speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TABLING OF COMMUNIQUE-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to table two copies in English-1 regret that it has not been possible yet to translate it into French- of a communique of the meeting of the Commonwealth Prime Ministers which has just concluded in London. This is a long communique covering a variety of subjects, because there were a variety of subjects on the agenda. I could, of course, make quite a lengthy statement on the communique. Perhaps it would be the wish of the Members of the House that this report appear as an appendix to Hansard so that all hon. Members would have an opportunity to study it. There might be an opportunity later for a discussion of the communique in the Committee on External Affairs or in the House.
Perhaps at this moment I could say only this, Mr. Speaker. There were two subjects which dominated the discussions. One was the proposal made by the Chairman of the Conference, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, on the opening day of the Conference, that the Commonwealth should choose certain of its members to initiate, if they could, by visits to the countries and the interests concerned, negotiations for a peace settlement in Viet Nam. That caused a good deal of discussion. Eventually there was agreement with regard to the personnel of the mission and the terms of reference of the mission.
I do not know whether this mission will be able to accomplish what it has in mind. It was an initiative taken by the Commonwealth, I think a valuable one and a timely one, par-

ticularly in view of the fact that it is not possible, at this time at least, for the Secretary General of the United Nations to take an initiative, or indeed any other international organization. Even if the mission itself is not able to accomplish what it hopes to accomplish, I do believe that the effort was well worth making.
The other major matter, major only in the sense that it caused a great deal of discussion and indeed some controversy, was that part of the communique which deals with Rhodesia. After long and very vigorous discussion the paragraphs on Rhodesia included in the communique were agreed to by all the members of the Commonwealth except one, who made reservation in connection with this particular section.
The importance of the Rhodesian paragraphs is that the Commonwealth members themselves, all of them without exception, came to the conclusion that there could be no final solution of this very difficult problem except on the basis of majority rule. The difference was over the timing of the processes which would lead to that final settlement. The United Kingdom Government, which have the responsibility of leading the people of Rhodesia to independence and majority rule, have accepted these principles in theory, and they have agreed-and this represents, I think, a pretty courageous advance on the part of the United Kingdom Government-if direct negotiations break down, to consider a constitutional conference, which is what the African members of the Commonwealth have been advocating.
I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that this was not only the largest of the Commonwealth Conferences, there being 21 members, but we learned at this Conference that at the next meeting, whenever it will be held, there will be four or five new Commonwealth members. It was a very difficult Conference, and in view of the difficulties and importance of the subject matters which were discussed we can take some satisfaction from the fact that this meeting was able to agree on a communique of this kind and, more important, was able to discuss such difficult and controversial matters in that spirit which characterizes Commonwealth meetings, even in respect to subjects on which it is not always easy and indeed is sometimes impossible to find unanimous agreement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not yet had an opportunity of reading the communique; the excerpts which were in the press were not complete. However, there are one or two references that I should like to make.
The first is to welcome the Prime Minister back to the House after a long and arduous meeting. No one who has participated in Prime Ministers' Commonwealth Conferences can forget that they are periods of very strenuous effort and work; and the fact that a communique was able to be determined upon is a further compliment to the Commonwealth and its representatives. The Prime Minister has said it was the largest Commonwealth meeting that has ever taken place. In 1957, as I recall it, there were nine members. Today there are 21, the large majority of whom are of another race, colour and religion to those ordinarily associated with the white continents.
I say at once that while the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom has spoken of the success of this Conference in rather eulogistic terms, my own feeling is that this Conference indicates once more the tremendous power of the Commonwealth and its membership in being able to achieve agreement in those larger things of life, while at the same time maintaining a sense of independence on the part of each of those who belong thereto. That it is a flexible institution is again revealed in the fact that the communique which has been issued illustrates that out of disagreement they have been able to arrive at a reasonable consensus.
While I did feel that in the intervening years between 1957 and 1962 there was among certain sections of the United Kingdom a diminishing belief in the mission of Commonwealth, recent events of the last session do indicate that much has been achieved. One has only to compare the meeting of the Prime Ministers with the collapse of the Algerian conference on the tenth anniversary of Bandung to realize that something of first importance to peace and the world brotherhood has been achieved by this Conference, a continuation of the results that were achieved at the previous Conferences. On the other hand, when you realize that after the war there were five white Christian nations and that today the membership of this unex-
Commonwealth Conference Report plainable institution consists overwhelmingly of those of other religious faiths, the ability to bring them together under the Crown, whether as monarchies or in the capacity of heads of the Commonwealth, is a triumph of statesmanship in the British tradition.
It is hard to explain that institution and I suppose no one will ever be able to do so; that is, how to bring together people with so many dissimilar views who are able to achieve something in the nature of a communique. Indeed, I was of those who felt that the day of communiques on the part of the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference was over. I thought the general attitude of the various nations making up the Commonwealth would lead to a condition of affairs that would at best be exemplified by discussion rather than by agreement.
The Prime Minister did not go into very much detail today. He told us in a sketchy way something about the peace mission. I do not want to be critical in that connection but, if my information is correct, I think the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, before having launched this plan, should have discussed it in advance through diplomatic communications with the various nations of the Commonwealth. I am told that until the opening of the Conference or shortly before the commencement of the first session the only Prime Minister who had information thereon was Sir Robert Menzies, Prime Minister of Australia. That is not the way to make effective, strong and positive Commonwealth initiatives.
In its composition 1 think the mission failed in advance because of the refusal of the various capitals to accept the suggestion that an Asian representative should be invited. Without an Asian representative the potential authority of any such mission was materially reduced. It is apparent that during the course of discussion the original concept, which was that of a mission of inquiry, was changed, and that substituted therefor was the proposal for certain guidelines to solve the ever more serious situation that is developing in Viet Nam. The guidelines included, first, cessation of military action by both sides and, second, recognition of the Viet Cong as one of the parties to be considered and recognized as an entity.
I would be interested to know what the reaction of the United States President was to this proposal. Apparently it was discussed by him and the Prime Minister of Australia prior to the conference opening. Does the Government of the United States agree now
June 29, 1965

Commonwealth Conference Report that any conference that may be called for the purpose of discussing the matters in issue shall include the Viet Cong?
I think too that the mission was weakened in advance by having chosen as its Chairman the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom who, while entitled to every eulogy for having brought about something in the nature of a plan, in my opinion ought not to have been chosen as Chairman of such a mission. Indeed, I doubt very much that he should have been a member of the mission, in view of the strong stand he had taken in the Parliament of the United Kingdom in favour and in support of the stand taken by the United States in Viet Nam. There was a realization on his part that those who glibly criticize what the United States is doing have no alternative to offer, and that the withdrawal of the United States from South Viet Nam would mean danger to all of us who believe in freedom everywhere in the world. That has been the view of the socialist Government of the United Kingdom, and it is a view that is generally shared, I think, throughout the world.
Where do we go from here? I had hoped that the Prime Minister would give the House some lead in this connection. Is this peace mission dead or is it merely in a state of suspended animation? What further course is contemplated to meet the ever worsening situation? In the last few days the United States has added to the number of its men in the force there and yesterday, apparently for the first time, went on its own initiative against the Viet Cong. That can only lead to more serious developments, and I would have hoped the Prime Minister would not have been so careful in the number of words he used so that we might have had some idea of the viewpoint of the Prime Ministers of the Commonwealth regarding a situation that shows no sign of improvement. Indeed, in the last few days it has revealed potentially dangerous steps which can only lead to an escalation in the face of which the world stands in awe and fear.
So far as Rhodesia is concerned, we are not very clear as to what was the viewpoint advanced by the Government of Canada. The Prime Minister said there was general agreement that a conference should be convened, apparently on the basis of universal suffrage. Was that Canada's viewpoint? What are the hopes that this problem will be capable of solution before it brings about in its wake frightening possibilities in all of Africa? What 

of last year's grandiloquent words in the communique regarding Rhodesia?
Everything seemed to have been reasonably and basically solved by last year's communique, but now we are in a position where the British government is back in the picture as fully as it always was. But there is nothing in this year's communique to make most clear and definite that the Rhodesian problem will be solved in a way that is fair and reasonable to white and black alike.
There are other matters to which reference could have been made, but I say with the greatest frankness to the Prime Minister that those two matters, Rhodesia and the peace mission, lack on his part the information that should have been given to Parliament so that we in this House may not have to depend entirely on press releases or communiques.
Because of other events of this day, such as the bringing down of the Royal Commission report, I can only hope that so important a matter as the position of the Commonwealth in the world of today should not receive the scant consideration which it did on this occasion on the part of the Prime Minister.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all welcome the Prime Minister back from what I am sure must have been a very strenuous and difficult conference of the Commonwealth Prime Ministers.
I must say I am disappointed that he did not give us more information in tabling this communique, but it may be his intention on interim supply, or some time during the next few days, to elaborate further on what took place at the Conference. I certainly wish he had been less casual and less uncommunicative on a number of matters which are of great interest to this House and to the people of Canada, such as the matter of Commonwealth trade, the matter of the Commonwealth secretariat, and further elaboration about Rhodesia.
We certainly ought to have some statement from the Government before the House recesses, with respect to the situation in Viet Nam. The mission set up by the Prime Ministers' Conference was, in my opinion, a bold and imaginative step. It is to be regretted that the Prime Minister of Ceylon, because of ill health, was not able to be a member of that mission, and I trust it is the intention of the Commonwealth Prime Ministers to invite one of the Asiatic Commonwealth Prime Ministers to act on the mission.
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped the Prime Minister would not only elaborate on the role
June 29, 1965	COMMONS
of this mission to deal with the Viet Nam situation, but that he would make some ringing affirmation regarding Canada's position in this very difficult and dangerous situation. The guidelines which have been set down in the communique are a great step forward, and certainly go much further than anything the Prime Minister has said here in the House or that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has expressed before the House or before the Committee on External Affairs. This communique recognizes something which the Government of Canada has constantly failed to recognize, namely that President Johnson's reiteration of the fact that he is in favour of unconditional peace negotiations has always been qualified, first by the fact that he was not prepared to sit down and negotiate with the Viet Cong, and second that he was not prepared to accept the basic tenet of the Geneva agreement which said that the boundary between North and South Viet Nam is provisional and that if the people want to express their opinions in free vote there is to be the opportunity to unify Viet Nam.
This communique at least recognizes those two important provisos which the President of the United States has always interposed When talking about unconditional peace negotiations. I would have like to see the Prime Minister say today that the Government of Canada espouses and supports the guidelines that have been established at the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference.
As hon. Members well know, the Prime Ministers suggested that the ultimate objective of this mission on the Viet Nam situation was threefold; first, a suspension of all United States air attacks on Viet Nam; second, to get North Viet Nam to undertake to prevent all movement of military forces and assistance to South Viet Nam; and third, a cease fire on the part of all parties pending a conference.
They also set forth four objectives for such a conference; first, the end of the war in Viet Nam; second, the withdrawal of all foreign troops in Viet Nam and the neutralization of the area; third, an international peace force set up under the Geneva accord powers to safeguard the peace in Viet Nam; and fourth, the eventual unification of Viet Nam through free and internationally supervised elections. These, Mr. Speaker, are the kind of guidelines and objectives which are realistic. They are the kind of guidelines that ought to appeal to both sides in this conflict.
I think before this recess the Government of Canada and if possible the Parliament of Canada ought to endorse these proposals. I 22620-190
DEBATES	2991
Commonwealth Conference Report think the Government of Canada should make a special appeal, either on its own behalf or by a resolution of this Parliament, asking the United States to take the first step which is a prelude to all the other steps, namely to suspend all bombing of North Viet Nam. There cannot be any hope for discussions or negotiations with a country which day after day is watching its towns, cities and installations being bombed and its people being killed. The other night over the C.B.C. someone who had been in Viet Nam gave it as his opinion that three out of every four persons being killed in North Viet Nam as a result of the bombing were women and children; civilians. If this is true, the resentment which must be building up in that country will in my opinion make it impossible to get any peaceful negotiations. If as a precedent to the rest of the objectives set down by the Prime Ministers' Conference the suspension of the bombing of North Viet Nam is placed first, I think the Government ought to say so and this Parliament ought to say so.
I am sure we all wish the Prime Ministers' mission on Viet Nam every success. I think we should recognize that the chance of their succeeding is very small unless they receive co-operation from both sides. It seems to me that the first step in this co-operation must come from our good friends and neighbours in the United States; it must be to discontinue the bombing as suggested by this communique.
I hope before we recess there will be further opportunities to refer to this subject so the Prime Minister can tell us something more about the Conference and, above all, so he can state categorically his own position in support of this communique, to the end that the world, and particularly the United States, may know that the Canadian Government and the Canadian Parliament are in support of these objectives, without which there seems to be little prospect of a solution being found. The fact that the Prime Ministers' Conference recognized the danger of escalation; the fact that it stated there seems to be no hope for a military solution; the fact that it concluded there must be a cease fire and a conference, all constitute a recognition that some breakthrough must be made. And the first step, it seems to me, is to get a cessation of the bombing as a prelude to a cessation of hostilities.

We join in welcoming the Prime Minister back in our midst. We have followed with great interest
2992	COMMONS
Commonwealth Conference Report the reports which have come to us of the proceedings at the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference. We are pleased that Canada is continuing to play a distinguished role as senior member of the Commonwealth and continuing to hold the respect of the newer members of the Commonwealth, as has been the case through recent years.
We are glad to have this copy of the communique. We wish a more detailed report could have been made with regard to what was accomplished and what went on during the deliberations of this Conference. I was disturbed to read in the press, and to hear over radio and television, speculation by some of our Commonwealth leaders about whether the Commonwealth could be held together. Indeed, there was a program broadcast by the C.B.C. on Sunday night, I believe, in the course of which the Prime Minister was interviewed, and the right hon. gentleman was reported to have said it would be a difficult task to prevent the Commonwealth from disintegrating. Remarks such as these characterize the situation which is prevalent in the world today.
I think there is something we should all realize when we try to define and understand just what the Commonwealth is; that is, when we think of the basic ingredients which brought the Commonwealth into existence and which account for the influence it exercises among its members and in a wider field. I am convinced that the reason the Commonwealth came into existence, and the reason it will continue to play a vital role, is simply that it is founded on the greatest heritage that we in the Commonwealth enjoy, namely the concepts of parliamentary government, British justice and freedom.

These characteristics of responsible, representative Government are the very warp and woof that go to make up the Commonwealth. While in the present world situation we may well be concerned about the problems we face, we should take courage from the fact that these principles will apply, on our part, to the solution of these problems.
We have listened with interest to the statements made by hon. Members who have spoken, particularly as they relate to the decision to form a Commonwealth Viet Nam peace mission. I think the Commonwealth has been courageous in moving forward on this issue. I join the hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in doubting whether much will

be accomplished by this mission. Certainly not very much can be achieved until there is a willingness on both sides to come together around the negotiation table. I do not know to what extent the prospects of the mission will be improved by lengthy expressions of opinions in this House, but I am sure it is the desire of all of us that it should achieve great success even though the prospects at the present time are not promising. Whether or not the peace mission succeeds, I am sure the effort itself will prove worth while. As such it will be one of the most important results of this recent Conference.
I think I should also refer briefly to the Rhodesian problem. It is encouraging to see that the communique again endorses without hesitation those basic principles which guarantee the rights of human dignity and respect to every person regardless of the colour of his skin or the creed in which he believes. This is a good thing. We recognize that the problem in Rhodesia is not a simple one. We recognize that its solution will not depend upon the wishes of the Commonwealth members alone, because the Government of Rhodesia is obviously determined to carry through the policies it has so definitely announced.
It is important to note that the Conference spent some time discussing economic affairs. One of our greatest responsibilities in the Commonwealth today is to exercise leadership in assisting the emerging nations to raise the living standards of their people. Certainly this is one of the great challenges which we face, and it is in this field of economic development that the Commonwealth has a tremendous, positive responsibility.
There is something in this communique that we have not had time to discuss in detail which I think is worthy of mention. Neither the Prime Minister nor any of those who have spoken have mentioned it. I refer to the agreed memorandum regarding the Commonwealth Foundation. I think each one of us ought to take this part of the communique and study it carefully, because here is one of the very positive programs with which the Commonwealth Prime Ministers dealt. I think it represents one of the most vital programs as far as the Commonwealth is concerned and certainly is of tremendous importance as we seek to raise the standard of economic development and of living in general for those people who live in what we tend to define as underprivileged areas.
This leads me to raise the question of the Commonwealth Secretariat. I think Canada
June 29. 1965

should be commended for understanding that the Commonwealth of the future may have a different form than the Commonwealth of the past, and for having taken the lead in offering one of our most distinguished diplomats to serve as Secretary General of that Secretariat. I commend the Government and the Prime Minister for being willing to part with the services of such an important man as Mr. Arnold Smith has been in our own area of external affairs-I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs understands this as well as anybody-in seconding him to an even greater service, one that will serve not only Canada but every part of the Commonwealth. We wish him all the success possible in this very difficult assignment as he plows forward into new ground, developing new policies and laying out a new foundation that I am sure is going to be the heart throb of the Commonwealth in the future. I think we have something to be proud of in this regard, and when I say that I wish Mr. Smith well I am sure all hon. Members of this House heartily ascribe to those good wishes.
So, Mr. Speaker, while we would like to have had a more detailed report from the Prime Minister, and I think it is important that such a report be given, we are grateful for what has been done and for receiving this communique, and we look with confidence to a future that is not all clouds and problems and does hold hope for something better.

Mr. Speaker, we have not had too much time to review the press release just distributed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). However, I want to express to him my greatest and best wishes on his return from London.
He has stated Canada's views over there and those views were highly appreciated by all the prime ministers attending that meeting of Commonwealth leaders.
When the Canadian Prime Minister took a stand on the Viet Nam conflict, for instance, he was appreciated not only in his own country, but by other Commonwealth prime ministers as well, because the logical position to take was to request a cease-fire in Viet Nam.
Now, according to the communique we have just received, we see the Prime Ministers discussed several matters: Malaysia, the Cyprus situation, Africa, Guinea, the West Indies, disarmament, Rhodesia, the territories belonging to the British Empire or the commonwealth. The economic situation not only 22620-1901
International Labour Conference within the commonwealth but throughout the world was also dealt with.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the United States err, as we of the British Commonwealth also do, when giving assistance to underdeveloped nations, in that while providing help we try to impose our way of life, our habits and customs upon them. And that is a gross error. I have often said that you cannot make white out of black or black out of white, but it is easy to respect both. Here, in Canada, there is talk about biculturalism, bilingualism, two cultures, etc. I often had the opportunity of saying across Canada that you cannot make a French Canadian out of an English Canadian or an English Canadian out of a French Canadian, but that you can make two good Canadians out of those two elements forming our country.
Now, when helping underdeveloped countries, a monumental error is committed in trying to have those people live according to our own way of life. If we give them technical assistance, technical knowledge, education, means to live their own lives, they will then have become our friends. I sincerely believe that the present Prime Minister shares that opinion, for he has made many statements in Canada along those lines in western as well as in eastern Canada, and I believe he shares the view that we must give those people, while letting them be themselves, the means to live decently, to rely on themselves as much as they are able to and to develop according to their own aspirations.
Then, the individual, the human person is respected from the economic standpoint. And while helping those countries we shall help ourselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with article 19 of the constitution of the International Labour Organization, I wish to table the texts in English and French of the instruments adopted at the 48th International Labour Conference held in Geneva, Switzerland, in June and July, 1964. The instruments consist of three international labour conventions and three recommendations.
The constitution of the I.L.O. requires a member state to bring conventions and recommendations "before the authority or authorities within whose competence the
2994	COMMONS
Inquiries of the Ministry matter lies tor the enactment of legislation or other action". In the case of a federal state there is the further obligation to refer instruments which are wholly or partially provincial in legislative jurisdiction to appropriate provincial authorities "for the enactment of legislation or other action", and to arrange for periodic consultations with a view to promoting co-ordinated action to give effect to the provisions of the instruments.
The opinion of the Minister of Justice, a copy of which I am tabling, is that each of the six instruments adopted last July is partially within federal legislative jurisdiction and partially within provincial jurisdiction.
The instruments include a convention and a recommendation on hygiene in commerce and offices, designed to protect the health of workers in commercial establishments and offices, and a convention and a recommendation on benefits in the case of employment injury. Although these matters are well covered in Canadian legislation and practice, there is not complete compliance at present in all jurisdictions with every article in the two conventions. Steps are being taken to explore with the provinces what action might be taken to ensure that all Canadian legislation and practice comply with the conventions, in the hope that they may then be ratified.
The remaining instruments are a convention and a recommendation on employment policy. On the basis of policies followed within the federal and provincial jurisdictions, we believe it is both possible and desirable for Canada to ratify the Employment Policy Convention. We are consulting with the provinces with a view to taking action on this convention at an early date.
As regards the three recommendations adopted by the conference, the question of ratification does not arise, since the I.L.O. constitution does not provide for ratification of recommendations. These instruments set forth standards as a guide for member countries. They will be referred to the appropriate authorities, and I am sure will be studied and found useful at both the federal and provincial levels.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the hon. Member for bringing this important matter to the attention of the House. The Minister of Agriculture for Canada met with the Ministers of Agriculture for Ontario and Quebec for two and one half hours yesterday, and I understand that those discussions were very fruitful.
Preliminary estimates indicate that some 14 countries are affected in Ontario and about 10 in Quebec. Agreement was reached as to the seriousness of the situation, and as to the

need for assistance to farmers who have suffered losses as a result of the dry weather.

speechtext:
that the House go into Committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the payment of development grants to assist the establishment of new manufacturing or processing facilities and the expansion of existing manufacturing or processing facilities in order to improve industrial employment opportunities in designated areas in Canada; for this purpose to establish in the Consolidated Revenue Fund an Area Development Account to which shall be credited an initial amount of fifty million dollars; and to effect certain related amendments to the Income Tax Act concerning the definition of a manufacturing or processing business and the application of section 71A of that Act in any case where a

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the House will recall that on June 7 the Prime Minister proposed certain major changes in the program of incentives for area development designed to broaden it and make it more effective.
The present measures for area development were introduced almost two years ago in recognition of the fact that certain areas of Canada had not achieved the measure of economic progress obtaining in the country as a whole. In these areas employment opportunities and levels of income are well below those enjoyed by most other Canadians. It is the policy of the Government in its campaign against poverty and inadequate opportunities to bring the benefits of industrial development to such areas in so far as it is possbile to achieve this.
As hon. Members know, the incentives provided under the present area development program take the form of accelerated capital cost allowances and a remission of income taxes. This program has had a substantial measure of success, and 1 would hope to have an opportunity during the discussion of the new legislation to describe some of its positive results.
Experience has shown us that a tax holiday is of benefit mainly to those firms which were able to reach a profit position at an early date in their operations. Other firms have to provide for market development and other settling-in costs during their first years of operation. Accordingly their profit position in the early years is such that tax benefits provide only a limited incentive. Moreover, we found that smaller firms in particular of a type well adapted to these areas experienced difficulties in initial financing.
For these reasons the Government is proposing to offer cash grants to new manufacturing and processing firms establishing in designated areas, as well as to firms expanding their existing facilities. The amounts of these grants are to be directly related to the total investment in fixed assets made by these enterprises. A firm which qualifies for a grant may elect to take it in the form of a credit against its income tax liabilities.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The legislation will provide funds for the payment of development grants. It will establish a formula to determine the amount of


grant to be provided to individual enterprises. It will provide that such grants will not be taxable income and will not be deducted from capital costs for tax purposes. It will amend certain provisions of the Income Tax Act concerning the definition of a manufacturing or processing enterprise, and the application of that act to development assistance. There is also provision for close liaison between the firms receiving development grants and the National Employment Service to ensure that the new employment opportunities are fully exploited and the appropriate training facilities established.
Finally, the Act will provide for regulations which will define in more detail the conditions and procedures for the payment of development grants.
Mr. Chairman, I hope to have a further opportunity to speak on this subject when the bill is before the House. My brief remarks at this time on the resolution will, I hope, indicate our firm belief that it is through positive measures of this kind that we will help to ensure that the employment and income opportunities generated by our expanding economy will be shared by all Canadians.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
We listened with interest to the Minister's introductory remarks concerning this resolution preceding a bill to be introduced asking that this house approve the setting up of a fund amounting to some $50 million in the consolidated revenue account from which the Department of Industry will be able to pay various amounts to industries which agree to establish themselves in designated or depressed areas.
As the Minister told us, it is only a little over a year ago that he introduced legislation designed to entice industry to locate in such areas. I think we all recall the problems which this legislation created in various areas of this country. I have no difficulty in recalling the problems created in my area. We were only 20 or 30 miles from a designated area, and the designated area began stealing our industries. In other words it became a matter of moving jobs from one area to another. I think the hon. Member for Renfrew had a similar experience; he had a designated area just across the border. The hon. Member for Brant-Haldimand also had a similar experience.
As a result this legislation did not meet with any large degree of approval. The Minister told these industries, we will give you certain concessions; we will not collect
June 29, 1S65

taxes for three years. Fifty per cent of the capital cost of machinery and equipment was to be forgiven, along with 20 per cent of the cumulative capital cost of all buildings. These arrangements did not work out satisfactorily. Now the Minister wants to put another patch on this patchwork quilt he began in December, 1963, but this time he is ready to hand out cash; this time a giveaway program, by means of outright grants.
I do not think that we as guardians of the Queen's purse have any right to give money in grants in this way. I would be in favour of making loans with interest. Making outright grants is a most unusual way of inducing industries to settle in depressed areas. We support the resolution in principle. We realize there are areas in Canada where economic growth is slow and that some assistance has to be provided. Nevertheless, I think we should ask ourselves whether this is constitutionally sound. Is it the business of the Federal Government to be in this particular field, or should this be an area in which the provincial authorities or the municipalities should operate? In connection with the former legislation there was often serious confusion and overlapping. There was uncertainty about who had the constitutional right to work in this particular sphere.
I could give many examples of the way in which provinces have gone all out to attract new industry. A heading in this week's Financial Post reads "Manitoba tosses more dollars into its pot to lure industries". The first paragraph says:
A five year plan to lure new industries, backed by government guarantee of an additional $100 million for the Manitoba Development Funds has been announced by Premier Roblin.
Ontario has embarked upon an extensive program to attract industry. And so it goes. I think this proposal before us is just another case of overlapping, another case of duplication. It is a means of spending the taxpayers' money in a way in which it should not be spent. I sometimes think it is a means of finding work for the 300-odd people who have been hired to staff the Department of Industry, one of the policies which have been dreamed up by the Department for that purpose.
This area development program is not original. It is nothing more than another program which has been copied from the United States. The Liberal Government has come out with a war on poverty, copied from the United States. The Minister of Labour went down to see U.S. Secretary Wirtz to
Grants to Designated Areas discuss with him how the problem of the displaced auto workers could best be handled. He came back with the program announced in this House yesterday. It seems to me Members opposite have copied one idea after another from the United States. Let us have Canadian policies for Canada; let us have policies for Canadians and draft them here, instead of going south of the border to get ideas. I am convinced that this legislation will come back to haunt the Minister in the years to come.
One of the things we can do as an opposition is to call the Minister's attention to some of the pitfalls which have been revealed in this program as it was instituted in the United States four years ago. As a matter of fact it was one of the first policies to which the late President John Kennedy put his signature in his war against poverty when he signed the legislation known as ARA; the letters stand for "area redevelopment administration". Today the Minister has introduced similar legislation, only he calls it "area development". The ARA as it was instituted in the United States four years ago contained some deep pitfalls into which the Americans have fallen. We in Canada under our program will find ourselves in the same situation. I have in my hand an article which appeared in the Reader's Digest of May, 1964.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The heading is "Is this the way to fight the war against poverty?" Then it says:
The Area Redevelopment Administration was set up lor a highly worthy purpose. But look at the way this U.S. agency is squandering taxpayer dollars-and callously ignoring the rights of individual citizens.
The article goes on to say:
For the ARA has. in the name of helping the poor, become the spearhead of one of the most outrageous government encroachments on private enterprise in United States history.
All we need to do is substitute "ARA" by "area development" here in Canada, and five years from now I am quite sure this article will fit the situation in this country. This article continues:
-ARA has uncoiled into a monstrous complex of co-operating bureaucracies. These agencies have dragooned or enticed a third of the nation's counties and 42 million of its citizens into accepting the label of poverty-
The article goes am
-ARA is riddled with bungling, political pressures and untold finagling.
I can just see it happening here, Mr. Minister. Then the article says:
June 29, 1965

Grants to Designated Areas
New installations are being financed by ARA in industries already beset by overcapacity, thus jeopardizing existing jobs.
It goes on to say that ARA is financing by means of a loan the expansion of the Howard Johnson chain of restaurants, and is thereby putting a great many private individuals out of business. It has loaned money for the building of new hotels, motels and so on. Another passage in this article is:
Areas that are far from "depressed" are getting help.
So through political finagling we find areas getting help when they are really not depressed. This article goes on to say:
Jobs constitute the only excuse for ARA's existence, but the agency provides brazenly inaccurate figures about the employment it generates.
I think we could apply these words to some of the figures and statements that have been made in this House as to the improvement that has taken place in the so-called designated areas here in Canada. To conclude these quotations, Mr. Chairman, I will quote what was said by two Senators of the United States, in which country they have had a plan similar to the one introduced by the Minister in respect of which he is now asking us to provide $50 million to support this program. Senator A. Willis Robertson of Virginia said this:
ARA Is an unsound spending scheme through which bureaucrats may make or break cities and towns all over the country by granting or withholding federal money.
Senator Frank J. Lausche said this:
This program is not economically sound. It is not fair to the taxpayers. It is a vote-buying device.
Oh, Mr. Chairman, I can see it happening here in Canada as I read those words. I can just see these depressed areas in which industries have moved in, and a big sign put up by the member of that riding saying "I brought this industry here. Vote for me in the next election". I can see the political implications of this program in respect of which the Minister is asking us to put up $50 million; and the next time he comes to Parliament with the program he will be asking for $100 million, not $50 million.
I mention this, Mr. Chairman, because it is bound to happen here. It happened there. This designated area program as it is set up is based on the N.E.S. office areas, and as hon. Members know these areas have certain boundaries. They are rather small, and the adjoining N.E.S. area may not be designated. There is still nothing in the legislation to change this overlapping and this proximity

of one area to another, or to take care of the great problem that we experienced before in this regard. I think the Minister should give consideration to using the Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures instead of N.E.S. areas as the basis of designation.
As I said before, this matter of grants is a bad principle. I am the first to admit that when we were in power as the Government we gave an outright grant to the Britannia Copper Mine in British Columbia. A very, very sincere plea was put forward at that time by the former Minister of Fisheries, Mr. Sinclair. I can see him yet, as I sat over there and he stood up with an envelope in his hand on which were written a few notes. He made a tremendous plea for a grant to the Britannia Copper Mine. Our Government gave this outright grant to the Britannia Copper Mine, and the result is that today the mine is closed. The outright grant proved to be not the proper thing to do.
I say again, Mr. Chairman, that I am not in favour of outright grants. We are in favour of loans with interest, and a personal stake by industry with regard to assistance. This resolution provides for the expansion of existing plants. It does not say whether the expansion of existing plants means that they can relocate in another area. This might be one method of expansion. They could exist in town A and expand by moving over to town B. If this were the case it would be just a transfer of jobs from one area to another.
Another thing I think should be mentioned here is that only in cases where private financing is not available should these grants be made. Then there is the matter of a community accepting the label of "poverty" or "depressed". I do not think any community wants to be labelled a poverty area. In my opinion this is bad terminology. I am one of those who believe that when you create the proper environment industry will move in and expand. I would say to this Government that they could go a long way toward creating a proper environment if they would remove the 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
This is the first step they should take. This would create a better environment for industries in these areas. I think you could give industry pie in the sky yet they will not locate in a depressed area, because industries do not operate in that way. Industries that are going to locate in given areas call in experts and say to them "We
June 29, 1965

are interested in locating in Canada. Will you make a survey and give us the whole story as to whether we should locate there". They study such things as transportation costs, closeness of raw materials and many other factors. In other words, Mr. Chairman, if you can prove to industry that they can make a dollar they will be there before you can catch them; but you have to create that environment. If they can make a dollar, they will be in there.
Take any industry for example. Take, for instance, Canada Dry. Suppose you wanted Canada Dry to come into a depressed area. You could give them all these things the Minister wants to give in the way of grants, and so on; but unless the water in that locality is of the kind they need to make their product, they will not go to the area. The policy which the Minister put before us earlier has not been working properly, and I see little improvement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext: It is a case of putting the cart before the horse.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
It is another example of poorly thought out legislation. This Government are working in reverse; they back up, take a step forward and then two steps back. This was a patchwork quilt program that was introduced and the Minister is putting another patch on the quilt and is asking us to vote $50 million for outright grants to be given to industry to move into these designated or depressed areas.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I conclude, Mr. Chairman, by drawing to the Minister's attention once more the facts and conditions that existed in the United States when they introduced such a program in their war against poverty. We should pay particular attention to the results of that program in the United States. I hope when he produces the bill and the regulations accompanying the bill this will be spelled out in much greater detail, but I sincerely hope the Minister will give this matter second thoughts and the consideration it should have so that he will not have to ask the House to change legislation again in the short period of a little over a year, as is the case today.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, until the bill comes before the House it will not be possible for us to take a definitive stand on the proposed legislation. But unless the bill offers something a little more worth while than what we have seen so far, I for one, and I

Grants to Designated Areas think many in this party, would be opposed to it.
Two years ago the Department of Industry made provision for area development, and with disastrous results. I think there is something to be learned from this legislation, which is still in existence. It shows that the isolation of one community, it being declared a designated area, simply does not work. I hope when the bill is brought in it will indicate that the Government has taken another look at the experience of the past and that entire areas, perhaps entire provinces, will be declared designated areas so the faults that exist, or which existed in the previous legislation, will not reappear in the new legislation.
South Waterloo was very badly hurt by the old legislation, despite the Minister's assurance to the people of South Waterloo that he was hopeful that the program would be more beneficial to places like Galt than if there were no program. That hope did not materialize. As the Minister knows, industries moved out of Galt into an adjacent area. All those in the area from which I come feel that the designation of an area of that type was a grave error. It accomplished nothing. I think the basis on which the designation was made was wrong, and I am afraid the Minister is considering this criterion in the new legislation.
Galt had gone to a great deal of trouble and made many plans to develop an industrial section. It prepared municipal services in anticipation that its industries would stay and would grow and develop, only to find that some of them moved out, and moved out with impunity. The important thing to new industry in a municipal area is the pool of labour available, the skilled and necessary labour needed by industry for its operations. In this particular circumstance industry was able to move out and draw its labour, while the municipality which had lost the industry had to pay for the cost of the services and of looking after the schools.
The Minister is fully aware that residential assessments do not cover the cost of municipal services, and that the municipalities require industrial assessments as well. To operate the legislation as the Minister did in the past, when he encouraged industry to move from a municipality, with the Minister telling the municipality that the people were still going to live in the municipality, is no help at all, because municipalities need industrial assessments to underwrite the residential assessments.

One change which is going to be made will be of some help, and it is an acknowledgment that the previous legislation was not particularly effective. The Minister says these measures were of great benefit to companies in a profit position but were less helpful to new and smaller firms. These new proposals hope to obviate that difficulty. Nevertheless the same basic fault exists in this new legislation which existed in the old. The grants are still being made on the basis of capital investment.
If it is the Minister's and the Government's intention that this legislation be part of a campaign against poverty and inadequate opportunity, and if it is the purpose of the legislation to help cure unemployment, then I cannot see how giving grants based on capital investment relates to the problem of curing unemployment. I think there are instances where this may be the case but there are other instances where it will not be the case. If a grant is based on capital expenditure only it will encourage industries of the automated type, industries which do not require much labour, to take advantage of this situation.
In our opinion if incentives are to be offered they should be on the basis of increasing employment opportunities, and grants should be made on the basis of how much employment will be offered. Grants should be given to industries of a labour-intensive nature rather than to industries which are going to use them to write off large capital investments. If these large capital investments involve labour-intensive employment, fine; but if they do not, then I hope the Minister has an answer to that particular problem.
In this regard, on the second page of his statement I see the Minister has a slightly different criterion for existing plants. He speaks of the help which will be given to existing plants in designated areas provided the expansion contributes appreciably to improving incomes and employment opportunities in such areas. This makes a great deal more sense than his first statement that the grant will be based on the size of capital investment. I hope he will follow this through and make it a uniform provision in the bill.
There is also the acknowledgement that this type of legislation is not going to be enough, that other programs will have to be devised in conjunction with this legislation. We hope a sincere effort will be made to do this. Educational facilities must be provided. Industry will not go where there is not a pool of

DEBATES	June 29, 1965
skilled labour. Industry needs this pool of skilled labour. Industry needs assurances that there are schools and training projects in the area so as to ensure that its requirements for skilled labour will be met. I certainly hope that such a program will be brought in with this suggested legislation.
The Government proposes to establish four guidelines for the designation of areas, and again I think the Government is making a mistake in relying on statistical evidence only. This mistake was made in the area surrounding my riding.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I think part of the error arises because of the statistical method of determining what should be a designated area. The Minister referred to areas where unemployment is severe, and no one will argue with that idea. I hope the Minister will also look into the reason for that situation. If the severity of unemployment is related to a statistical fact, in that there are seasonal workers in the area, then his statistics will be completely wrong and his assumption that an industry will locate in that area will be incorrect.
The Minister speaks about areas where there has been a large and persistent decline in the number of people employed. We must do something more than simply say that if that is so we should designate this area. If there are root causes there for unemployment, such as that the area in question has no natural attractions and never will have for industry, by forcing industry into such an area we will only be inviting bankruptcy. The Minister will have to take a very close and careful look at this type of situation.
In respect of areas where unemployment is substantially above the national average, and the rate of increase in employment is substantially lower than the national average, here again this cannot be judged by statistics. A close look must be taken in respect of this area with some common sense exercised to determine whether the area has a future for industry and can sustain industry. We will not be doing anyone any favour by moving industry into such an area simply as a good short term solution, because we may wind up being shortsighted, playing a hoax on the people in this area, and leading them to believe that theirs is an area that can sustain and support an industry over a long period of time, particularly if that area has no natural advantages to offer an industry which must compete with other industries. If the Minister insists on doing this sort of thing
June 29, 1965	COMMONS
in a situation of this kind, then he and his Government must be prepared to continuously subsidize industry located in areas improperly prepared for them.
I am disappointed that in all these indications regarding designated areas the Minister has left out what to me is probably the most vital thing to be examined. Can industry prosper and sustain itself? These programs are fine and the kind that most people will not argue against in principle. I am sure every Member of this House wants to do something about chronic unemployment, but we must be careful that in our attempt to cure chronic unemployment, which could perhaps be cured much better and more adequately by other measures, we do not force industry into a position where it cannot compete so that in the long run this nation will not advance and prosper in all areas.
In order that all areas of this country can prosper we must assure ourselves that our competitive and productive position is good. We must not do anything which puts chains on industry. We must be very careful that this kind of legislation, even with the best of intentions, will not create a monster which will require permanent subsidization and will result in lower productivity and, in the long run, a lower standard of living for Canada.
When the bill following this resolution is presented to this House we must consider it to see whether the long run problems have been considered, whether it will do something to increase our productivity, and something to foster a higher standard of living in Canada. We must look to see whether this legislation fits into some kind of national plan, or whether it is only a sop for those who are making loud noises in certain areas. We must look to see whether it is going to be political or based on a carefully considered objective. We must look to see whether it embodies ideas which will really assist municipalities, or whether it will impose difficulties upon municipalities which become designated areas. Let us not forget that by forcing industry into these areas we could create a series of problems for the municipalities which they never dreamed they would have to face, as the result of an increased demand for services. In that event, instead of helping the municipalities or areas we might effectively destroy them by raising their tax rates as a result of forcing them into the position of having to supply services which were not required in the past and may not be required in the future, except in anticipation of growth that may never

Some excellent reports have been made available recently in respect of this subject. I have had the opportunity of reading the report prepared by the Atlantic Finance Research Board, under the direction of Professor T. Wilson of the University of Glasgow, about the Atlantic provinces. I was greatly impressed with what that report had to say about this situation, and particularly impressed with the argument advanced for regional designation as opposed to local designations accompanied by the location of small factories in this town, that own and another town.
The report suggests that that is the worst possible thing that could happen. It points out that what should be done is designation on a regional basis, so that people of the same background and historical attitude, without having to move far from their families, could become employed in the central area. Surely that is the way to improve and increase the total performance and standards of areas of high unemployment.
In this regard I am sure my colleagues will be a little more specific, and will relate their remarks to particular areas. We all look forward to the bill itself in order that we may ascertain those things included in the bill which will be of real help to Canada instead of just words without meaning.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to say categorically that I am not greatly impressed by the legislation anticipated by this resolution. If there ever was a situation where we were mistaken I think this is it, because even a novice taking one glance at the legislation can see that we are not being consistent and are not achieving anything so far as policy is concerned. In other words we are not doing anything really constructive.
I was interested in hearing the Minister state that these grants could apply against income tax liabilities. When the Minister gets up to reply I should like him to tell us why we should be interested in granting money to people who are in an income tax bracket. It does not make sense to me. Why should we be in the position of giving a grant to somebody who is in an income tax bracket? If they are going to pay a large amount of income tax they do not need these grants. People have their own methods of seeking out places to locate sound and good businesses.
June 29, 1965

Grants to Designated Areas
In this connection I might put in a plug for the City of Prince George. In the next few years $400 million is going to be spent within a radius of five miles of Prince George. Business people know a good place to go to establish and build up a business. We do not need this type of provision at all. For instance,
I think we might look into the action taken by the Town of Arnprior some years ago. I remember being in the railway committee room when an official from Arnprior explained what they had done. There are Members of the House of Commons who come from that area. The municipality itself established certain incentives to induce business firms to establish there on a permanent basis and thus provide the type of employment and expansion of business needed by the Town of Arnprior. When we were given this information in the railway committee room I was very much impressed with the way the municipality had undertaken to overcome the difficulties facing it. I say to the^ Minister that if there is any place where the Government should start giving assistance across Canada it is to the municipalities. This is where the Government should be giving assistance.
I was much impressed by most of the remarks of the last speaker. I think he showed he had a very good grasp of the whole situation with regard to this legislation. The purpose of industry in Canada or anywhere else is to produce goods and services, not to provide jobs. If the purpose of industry is to provide jobs then we had better revert to the situation that obtains in undeveloped countries. This morning I was talking to a newspaperman on the street and he said that in a country he had visited not long ago there would be perhaps 50,000 men working on a project that would be handled by five or six dozen men in Canada or the United States. If we want to reverse the trend and start to provide people with work for work's sake, then I say there should be an over-all policy in the Department of Forestry and other departments to clean up our forests and provide access roads for fire protection and so on. There are many places where people can be put to work.
The fact remains that if an industry is induced to move into a certain area there is no guarantee that the people of that area are going to get the jobs. I have a very clear recollection of a fairly large highway operation where the local people in the area were not hired to work on the highway at all. There
[Mr. Leboe.l

were many good catskinners and gradermen available who could have been used, but the unions had unemployed members in Vancouver, Winnipeg and other places. Because the contract specifically stated that union members would be used, these people were shipped in from other provinces and given first chance at the available jobs.
I am not complaining about that. These are the facts. But what guarantee has the Minister that if an industry is established in a particular area the people of that area will get the jobs? There is no guarantee whatsoever that the people of the area will benefit in that regard.
In addition, while we have not a very large population in Canada and while I maintain we should have a much larger population, the fact is that our population is large enough that there is great flexibility in the movement of the labour force. This has been proven to be so in the Province of British Columbia. In that province the labour force is growing and growing but so is unemployment. Why? Because people are moving there to get jobs. They know there are jobs available, but if two people go out there for every job available there is still going to be plenty of unemployment. It is a fact of life that people move to places where jobs are available. All people are not tied by their apron strings to one place. Certainly an emotional factor enters the picture when a family wants to stay together in the area where they are now living, but I say there is enough flexibility in the labour force that tremendous movement can take place.
The last point I should like to mention is the economic factor, which I believe is paramount. I do not think we should induce industries to locate in places where it will not be economically sound for them to operate and survive. If an industry is artificially stimulated to locate in a particular area, it is obvious that the death knell of that industry is a foregone conclusion. It will fail eventually.
Although I have not consulted other members of my party, I am sure they will agree with me when I say that this legislation is a piecemeal, patchwork approach to overcoming unemployment in depressed areas. Because of automation and the changes that are taking place the need arises for workers to move and, as was mentioned yesterday, we must have an over-all policy that will take care of any contingencies that may arise in the case of individuals. We must do this and forget about the business of trying to stimu-
June 29, 1965

late industry to locate in a place where economically it does not belong.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel I must enter the debate on the motion before us because it concerns industry. Canada experiences major problems in this field.
I wonder if the proposal to distribute $50 million in loans will increase industry in Canada to the extent of providing work for all people in designated areas. Is the distribution of money in designated areas intended to displace industries?
If we take industries out of Montreal and relocate them in a designated area, while people are already out of work in Montreal, this will not solve the unemployment problem. If the Montreal industries relocate in designated areas of the province, will there be work for present employees of such industries? Can the minister tell us whether, at this time, there is plenty of production in Canada, or whether there is a lack of it? If there is a lack of it, why do industries not produce?
You will reply that perhaps it is because they do not have the money. Why does the Canadian industry lack money? Well, I will tell you right now, Mr. Chairman, it is that instead of financing consumption, we finance production. I am sure that the fault is not with production, but with consumption, because at this time, in 1965, our total gross production will top $50 billion. Now, in 1964, we barely disposed of $35 billion worth of products. This means that the balance is in warehouses.
We have lots of needs in Canada. We have an abundance of needs and they are flagrant. But consumers do not have the money to buy the production. If production is increased, what problem will that solve? Will that production be held in storage or will it be used to serve the needs of Canadians?
Well, if the needs of the Canadian people are to be served, let us organize the Canadian economy.
Our economy is not balanced. There is a lack of equilibrium between production and distribution. So long as we fail to solve the problem of equilibrium between the two, it is useless to put amounts of money at the disposal of manufacturers and to pay excessive rates of interest on those amounts.
Who are we going to protect in doing so? Those who manipulate high finance, to the detriment of the consumer.

Grants to Designated Areas
At this time we already have excess products in storage, and such consumers as might buy them do not have the money to do so; they would have to borrow.
Therefore, we borrow to manufacture products and we also borrow to consume them. Where are we going with this sort of unbalanced economy? If we are unable to find a way to balance this system which is beyond the reach of the Canadian people, it is useless to try to administer the country.
If war were declared tomorrow, all kinds of means would be found to balance the budget; necessary steps would be taken so as to put the production on the market, because we would know that everything that is destroyed would have to be replaced.
But, at present, if you want to replace production by other products, you have to work in order to sell products for the welfare of human beings. Canadian families have needs. There are still, in many constituencies of Canada, families that do not have bathroom in the house. This does not mean they do not need them. The needs exist, but the people are unable to obtain the goods they need.
It is essential to find a way to stabilize this economic factor which has been lagging for years, in fact, ever since confederation. In the past we could say that we had production problems. But those problems have been eliminated; today we have no production problem, nor any transport problem, but we have some tremendous financial problems.
If we wish to finance production and try to give a new impetus to the economy in designated areas, this can not be done with loans, because they would only be another burden on the taxpayers' shoulders who would have to pay more interest. This would contribute to increase the cost of goods to such an extent that individuals would no longer be in a position to buy them.
What is the use of producing in that case? If we want to be logical, let us set up our economy on a balanced, scientific and businesslike basis. This will not be done through loans. Loans have been known for a long time; they are as old as the world. They should never have come into existence, yet they do exist. Some people insist that money should yield profits, whereas money does not bear returns. This explains the imbalance, and this problem must be solved.
Several areas of the country are going through a recession. Finance is to blame rather than producers, consumers or workers.
June 29, 1965

Grants to Designated Areas Let us solve the problem of finance and we shall then settle practically all problems. But the matter is being overlooked.
I asked earlier for an increase in family allowances in order to provide taxpayers with purchasing power. Some Liberal members laughed. You will laugh, you Liberals, in the face of families, in the face of those who are starving, at the next election.
You can go and laugh at them in their own countries. You have already done so. I do not know who did, but I heard about it. That is what goes on, Mr. Chairman. Some are satisfied with their salaries, are content to eat their fill, while others starve in Canada, starve in the Province of Quebec. To prevent them from starving, we need reforms, monetary reforms.
We shall get such reforms if you are willing to open your eyes and ears, to put your fingers on the evil that festers in our shaky economy, on the business failures that occur throughout the land. There are bankruptcies everywhere. Why are there so many? Because there is not enough money in circulation. People are unable to buy and industries cannot sell.
I am the owner of a small industry myself. The problem is not one of manufacturing but of sales. The problem in this country, as far as sales are concerned, is one of getting paid; that is the trouble and you refuse to settle the problem. The problem cannot be settled by loans.
If you want to settle the problem of the Canadian economy there is overstocking of real products on shelves-then why not give an adjusted discount on these products. This will result in products being sold at reasonable prices.
It is not interest on money that is needed. The sole purpose of the administration is to arrange for loans. The government has become a lending institution, it endorses loans, it endorses financiers, so that the latter may obtain 6, 7 and 8 per cent. That the people be taken unfair advantage of, that they be throttled, is not important, but interest on money must be maintained at any cost; governments must be endorsers and take their responsibilities toward the whole of Canada, they must endorse all those loans in order to organize the Canadian economy a little.
Some small industries are head over heels in debt even before they start operating. They cannot even go on operating because production is overtaxed-there are direct, indirect, provincial, municipal and school taxes, so

that production is taxed up to 50 per cent of its value. When you buy a piece of equipment or a piece of furniture, if the latter costs $100, taxes account for $50.
That is the kind of economy we would like to reform. It is not with the system advocated by the government that the present system will be corrected. A solution can be found. I said so a moment ago, it is by means of a compensated discount on products that this problem can be solved and, of course, with money from the Bank of Canada. There is surplus of production which the people need, which they should have and which they should be able to purchase.
In industries automation has now replaced the worker to a great extent. Where 100 men were employed before, only 10 are required now with automation. Industries are modernizing as never before.
Who is going to buy the production? I am asking you? Who is going to solve the problem of consumption in Canada? Production is financed, but nobody thinks about financing consumption. Consumption is a necessity of life and, consequently, first consideration should be given to financing the consumer not by indirect but by direct means, not by letting him be exploited by financiers but by helping him by direct means, so that the individual consumer can satisfy his own needs, for there is an abundance of production.
But production should be controlled by the consumer and not only by producers, because what is the use of producing if you cannot sell.
I would have a lot more to say, Mr. Chairman, but I will confine my remarks to what I have said. I am asking all those who are controlling the economy, ministers of the government, for instance, to introduce the necessary remedy in order to improve the lot of the Canadian people.
If Canadians do not get that, communism will spread in Canada. In fact, it is already permeating everywhere in Canada. Why? Because there is hardship in the country and the people have lost all hope of a better lot. The only thing which our citizens have are new troubles and new taxes. They are discouraged, they are no longer even interested in politics. At the last election, only 30 per cent of Montreal's electors voted, which shows how disenchanted citizens are with politics.
There are also urgent economic factors. The problem will not be solved only by setting up new industries to create more jobs. I am for new industries indeed, but I want us to
June 29. 1965	COMMONS
keep those we already have. The existing industries fight in a mess of problems. Only big industries and large capital get excessive profits. They suit large finance interests by borrowing money, but they have to charge prohibitive prices for their goods in order to pay the interest demanded by financing interests.
I thank you, Mr. Chairman. Once more I want to assure you of my appreciation. I would like to see the government take a positive step from an economic standpoint, from the standpoint of industry in Canada and from the standpoint of consumption in this country. Something needs to be done. We are not after power, because we are not here for that. We are for improvement. If those who preside over the destinies of this country make the improvements asked by the people, we will be the first to congratulate them. If they do not, we will continue to tell the people that there is no improvement and that the present government protects only a small group of society to the disadvantage of ail the others.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
