speechtext:
Let me say at the outset that I support the principle of this legislation. Some hon. Members have criticized the advisability of proceeding by means of grants as against tax incentives or tax reductions. Let me point out, having been in business, that there is a difference between the two: Before you get tax credits you must make a profit. The purpose of this legislation is in part to share the risk. It has been said on many occasions that the Government is a partner in the profits-why not in the risk?
Having said this, may I add that I find the resolution something of a paradox. I understand from the definition the Minister gave that these provisions only apply to manufacturing or processing facilities. I put it to the Minister that most of the areas designated are four-square with the tourist industry. Nevertheless, the tourist industry is not included in the definition. I am afraid we regard the tourist industry as not being an industry at all. Mr. Deutsch of the Economic Council has indicated that new jobs will have to be found in the service industries rather than in the manufacturing industries. I put it to the Minister that there is some help already available for manufacturing industries, while no help is available to the tourist industry of this country, to bring it up to date.
DEBATES	3011
Grants to Designated Areas
We should consider the fact that Canadians and Americans will have more time and more money to spend. Despite the many natural attractions of this country they will be reluctant to spend more of these dollars here until our facilities have been improved and brought up to date. Our operators do not have the money to make the necessary improvements. Consider the facilities which are available in New York State where the tourist industry has now become an important full time industry. To cater efficiently to the needs of tourists, local help is necessary, and this is a field which can probably be developed to even more profitable advantage than the relocation of manufacturing and processing.
I have no criticism to make of this measure. I think it will help the general economic situation. But I should like to call attention to the fact that the Government has neglected to include the tourist industry in its definition, and with great respect I suggest the Department of Industry should take another look at this industry, bearing in mind that it may be comparable in employment opportunities to the manufacturing and processing industries in the areas concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution under study gives me the opportunity to express my opinion and that of two so-called independent bodies, with regard to this measure. I hope the information I shall provide to the minister will help him correct, if possible, the inadequacies of this legislation. But before starting my remarks, I must say that I sympathize with the minister, because it must certainly be most distressing to be criticized by one's own political colleagues. I commend the previous speaker for his objectivity and I trust that the minister, contrary to what he has always done up to now, will take heed of his advice and act accordingly.
Mr. Chairman, I entirely support the opinion expressed a few moments ago by my colleague, the hon. Member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales). I think that, because of other similar measures taken by various governments, the present measure is only a duplication of what has been done by other governments; in fact, it is not entirely lacking in political sense and shows some understanding of what patronage can do for a government. In any case, I submit that this initial amount of $50 million seems very impressive and I am of the opinion that the
June 29, 1965

Grants to Designated Areas minister would be well advised to take note of any advice given him, particularly from this side of the house.
If you take a quick look at the various designated areas, you are bound to come to the conclusion that the Liberal ridings, especially those represented by cabinet ministers, are particularly well treated, and in that regard I will bring evidence only from people with nothing at stake in this matter, namely the mayor of St. Hyacinthe and the provincial Minister of Industry and Commerce, Mr. Gerard Levesque.
I cannot help notice that, to a similar extent, the government gives quite a special treatment to big companies and does not give the necessary consideration to small ones.
In my province, handicraft, small industry, family industry play a very important part and I believe that the minister should give particular consideration to that sector of industry. Small industry has played a very important role in the past and, because of the lack of consideration and support by the government, and because of competition on the part of big industries, those small local family companies find themselves in a very precarious position. Therefore, I beg the minister to grant this situation a special consideration in order to rectify, if necessary, the deficiencies of this resolution.
I was saying a moment ago that I would like to convey to hon. members the appreciation of the mayor of St. Hyacinthe and of the Quebec Minister of Industry and Commerce. I should like to quote part of an article published in Le Courrier on February 4, 1965:
If the city of St. Hyacinthe is in such a had state as far as industrial development is concerned, even though it is financially and administratively sound and in a position to provide many services to individuals as well as to institutions, the federal government at Ottawa is indirectly to blame because of the various areas it has considered as designated areas.
It goes on to say:
In short, that is the opinion expressed by His Honour Mayor Jacques Lafontaine, on Monday, to city council in connection with the annual brief presented by the central council of national unions and following his trip to Quebec City where he met, last Thursday, Mr. Gerard-D. Levesque, Minister of Industry and Commerce, to discuss the impossible situation of a city such as ours.
Everybody knows that our city lost several new industries to other municipalities, such as St. John and Shawinigan, to mention only those two.
Now, those cities are in so-called designated areas because of their high rate of unemployment, and their administrators are now able to give

extraordinary advantages to industries wishing to settle within their limits-
That is the opinion of the mayor of the City of St. Hyacinthe. But what is the opinion of the provincial minister of Industry and Commerce? Here it is:
The Quebec Minister of Industry and Commerce stated that normal cities are getting a poor deal but that the provincial government is not responsible, because it was not consulted in any way by the federal authorities which, on their own initiative, decided which were the designated areas in our province.
And the minister concluded:
As long as this deplorable state of affairs is maintained, the chances for industrial development in the province will be small, and the federal state is the only one to blame.
Mr. Chairman, in quoting the Quebec Minister of Industry and Commerce, I feel that I am repeating the remarks of a person who is not a political enemy of the federal Minister of Industry and I find it odd that a provincial Liberal minister should speak in such strong language about this federal Liberal government. It is surely because the Quebec Minister of Industry and Commerce felt justified in doing so when he visited St. Hyacinthe and also when the mayor of St. Hyacinthe went to Quebec City, and made the statement I have just quoted.
I wish the minister would devote a little more attention to the development of trade and commerce in our province and a little less attention to political patronage, which is beneficial only to his party.
I do hope that these words will give the minister food for thought and allow the municipalities in the province of Quebec, and more particularly the city of St. Hyacinthe, to obtain their fair share.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, representing a large area of northern Ontario where this type of legislation was considered to be very advantageous because of particular factors, I am very unhappy with the operation of this Act and with the whole operation of the Department of Industry which has administered the Act. It is a fact that there are areas of Canada that are in need beyond all others of government assistance in developing industry. You will remember, Mr. Chairman, the hue and cry that went up when the Prime Minister's area was hard hit with unemployment a year or two ago when they closed down the uranium industry as such. You will remember, also, that at that time
June 29, 1965

the Government had spent millions and millions of dollars in regard to that particular affair, for which the Liberal Party can take absolutely no credit but have to bear a great deal of blame, in the development of that industry.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Remember the community of Nickel Belt which supplied uranium to the United States. The town almost disintegrated overnight when this industry was no longer needed and Parliament was asked to designate it a distressed area. I think everyone in Canada agreed with this action because a large number of people were displaced and a terrific amount of capital wasted and squandered on the expectation that this mining community would continue for a number of years.
A number of people objected this afternoon to things which had happened in the past. I am aware that this type of incentive does produce anomalies in areas it is meant to help. We are all familiar with the situation in Brantford. Some of us are aware of the situation in the Waterloo area. We are aware of the fact that this legislation has caused many unpleasantries and much unhappiness between communities which have taken advantage of this legislation, and others which have not. Kirkland Lake is a good example of the type of area not considered. Renfrew is in no different position, as are a number of other locations in every province in Canada. These are communities which died slowly over a long period of time.
The industrial commission in Kirkland Lake went to see some government officials in Ottawa on two occasions on the question of assistance to develop secondary industry. The first time they were surprised that the Department of Labour did not have sole jurisdiction over deciding what should be the criterion, what the incentive program would be and how the designated areas were decided. They were surprised that the Department of Labour considered Kirkland Lake to be fairly well off because of two factors. One was that there was no unemployment, which is fairly easily understood. The other was that the total wealth per person in the area is not very great. I am wondering whether the township I live in is one of the most wealthy townships in the country, if that is the kind of statistic used. I may be one of the few taxpayers in my area, but because of the income I receive these statistics may indicate that this is a wealthy taxpaying area. Certainly the farmers in my area do not pay
Grants to Designated Areas much tax, so if this sort of criterion is used the situation becomes ridiculous. This may be happening with regard to Kirkland Lake.
With regard to the question of unemployment, we have an unemployment insurance office which several years ago was divided into branches, owing to the diversity of industry in the area covered. I thought this was fair and reasonable and worked to the advantage of the people it served. But it meant that the bush working population, which is a seasonally employed population, joined with the agricultural population and was transferred to the new unemployment insurance office at New Liskeard. The office at Kirkland Lake has been left with a stable work force, and therefore there is no unemployment.
You may be surprised to know that no young people register for employment at Kirkland Lake. This is because there are no jobs in Kirkland Lake available. These people know when they graduate from the institute in the area or from the vocational school or high school that if they are going to work, then they have to go to Toronto. Therefore they move to Toronto and get a job. They never register at Kirkland Lake. Perhaps we should have had everyone unemployed at Kirkland Lake register, and if this were done the unemployment figure would certainly triple immediately. These people are not stupid. They are well aware which jobs are available and they do not apply for jobs which do not exist. They do not want to become part of this statistic in which I see no sense.
Less than a year ago there was a bad accident in one of the mines in my area. These mines are over a mile in depth and have reached the economic limit of their productive capability. As soon as two men were killed last fall at one of the mines, it was closed. Two weeks ago there was a very bad bump at the Lakeshore mine and it was closed, except for salvage operations. This means that 600 people have been laid off. I have not been able to check the figures because I do not know where the figures will be found, but I bet that these 600 employees are probably one third of the total number of unemployed which Kirkland Lake had during the worst period over the last two or three years. I will bet that these 600 people do not register anywhere for employment, because the average age of the miners working in the gold mines at Kirkland Lake is 54. So where would they get a job? They have worked for 35 to 40 years underground in gold mines. Are they going to work on a farm or pick up a chain
June 29, 1965

Grants to Designated Areas saw and go into the bush? Are they going to become truck drivers or work on the railways? What kind of jobs can they apply for? So they do not register and become part of the statistics. Yet this Government is not smart enough to find some way to accommodate the people in that area who are not able to take advantage of employment in manufacturing industries and join the numbers who go to make up these statistics.
If any of these officials are in the galleries, there may be among them some of the smart young people who travel around, and I have met many of them. The Minister of Industry should be quite proud of the number of people he has been able to assemble, but they have not done a damned thing for places like Kirkland Lake. One official became quite interested in Kirkland Lake and I should like to read part of a letter which he wrote to the Kirkland Lake Industrial Commission after he returned to the Department. This young fellow was lent to the Prime Minister to help in the war on poverty. I do not know what that will mean, but there are many people in my area who would not consider Kirkland Lake to be a rapid growth area. They are well aware of the fact that Kirkland Lake, since its peak period between 1937 and 1942, has gone steadily downhill. This is what this official says:
Upon my return from Kirkland Lake, I conducted an Inquiry into the possibility of designating the territory administered by the National Employment Service Office of Kirkland Lake for the financial incentives program of the Area Development Agency and, as we had foreseen during our discussions last September, I found that there was no possibility of obtaining designation at that time. Moreover you will no doubt recall that I had indicated to you, during the same discussions, that the Area Development Agency Program for Designated Areas had been under review and that we would have to await the results of this review before further discussions along these lines could be entertained. This situation still exists. I do hope, however, that within a relatively short time we shall know whether or not the program, as it now exists, is to be modified.
At a further meeting we have had with them we were informed that it is not, and that this situation will not be corrected.
I believe that we should be more interested in people than in property. This is a capital incentive program. This program assists capital investment. It helps give to capital; but it really does not give to people. This is one of the most advantageous capital bolsters we have had for a long time, but it does not help the people to become employed in industry. We are merely adding incentive to capital; it is not given to people.

I am well aware there are other programs which do assist people, but this one does not. This program is a bolster to capitalists, something to which I have never dedicated myself, and I have never felt strongly about the capitalist system. Yet this Government gives $50 million to aid capital, having no regard for people or for communities which have been built up at terrific expense.
We have hospitals, schools, technical institutions, vocational schools, a dozen or more primary schools, a fire and police department equivalent to that employed by a community of 50,000 people, all paid for by 800 miners who are employed in that community. What is to be done about this situation? All the Minister suggests is that industry be located elsewhere, and we know that once industry is located in the suggested areas there will follow these increased demands for social capital. As one Member suggested, we are going to build these communities on the golden horseshoe basis.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Let us remember that we must keep industry close to the area of consumption. We all know, including the officials of the department, that there is not going to be a mill established to process the iron ore of northern Ontario because it is uneconomical. I do not think many people have complained about that fact, or about the fact that Jones and Laughlin is exporting the product to the United States, yet unable to build a steel mill in the Timiskaming area. Let us not forget, however, that we are not getting one red cent in royalties in this regard, but rather wages for 200 people. Has the Department of Industry given us any consideration because 300 people have been laid off this month? We have not been designated as a distressed area-hell, no. Instead of that, other areas where wages are 30 or 40 cents per hour higher have been so designated.
Timmins has been designated as a distressed area and the situation there is no different from that of Kirkland Lake, in spite of the fact that the situation in Timmins has changed considerably since the stock market took a jump. There are those who say we are not going to have a smelter in Timmins, but let me assure you that the people in the Timmins area will not continue to mine or sell their Texas-Gulf for export to the United States. We are interested in getting benefits equal to those received by other areas, and Kirkland Lake is not receiving equal benefits.
June 29, 1965

There is no justification for anyone who has half an eye, driven through that area and observed the situation there, wanting to create another Cobalt there.
Throughout northern Ontario and northern Quebec communities the people are having to provide increased capital services such as roads, sewers, sidewalks, police and fire protection. The people of those areas have provided the capital which has built and maintained the services to this time, and they deserve some assistance in the maintenance of those social capital expenditures, particularly when industry no longer exists. Other countries like Sweden have been able to develop initiatives in this field in deciding where industry should be located. They have been able to sit down and plan their economy.
You know yourself, Mr. Chairman, as a result of driving in the Toronto area that the many factories there this month which were not there last month require greatly expanded social capital services, and that this expansion of industry will require an equivalent expansion in transportation. These problems are always magnified by increases in industrial locations in an area.
Who was it provided the capital for the development of Elliot Lake? The federal Government provided $90 million for that area in the form of cash and tax exemptions for mining companies over a three-year period. Some of these companies did not spend one red cent in the development of this area. The Canadian Government supplied the money to build these plants. The situation has not proved economical so far as the miners are concerned. They spent their savings, worked there for a period of a few years and then had to move out, losing everything they had invested. Has the Department of Labour or the Department of Industry taken this into account?
The Minister of Industry and the Minister of Labour are well aware of the circumstances surrounding these mining areas, and every official of those departments knows of the situation that now exists. I refer to areas in the proximity of Renfrew, the head of the Lakes, particularly around Port Arthur, as well as other areas developed in the north because of an abundance of primary products, whether utilized by the forestry or mining industries.
If we are going to check this developing problem, it must be done now rather than wait for 150 years as was the case in the Maritime Provinces. Let me warn this House now that if there is any intention to pass
Grants to Designated Areas this legislation by July 1 without some consideration being given to the areas I have mentioned, if I can find any way to stop it, there will not be an adjournment for the summer recess for at least a month. The people of northern Ontario are worried about the situation and feel that steps should be taken to make their conditions at least equal to those of other similar areas.
Within the next two years there will be no gold mines left in northern Ontario. Surely the Minister cannot say that he is not interested in that fact. The Government of Canada has paid $10 million per year toward assisting the gold mining industry in these northern communities. Are they now to be abandoned? If that is the attitude taken by this Government, then what they are doing is honouring only the financial interests of the gold mining industry, the shareholders and others connected with this development, and disregarding the interests of the people who work in the industry. Is the Government prepared to say that? If it is not prepared to do so, then I suggest some change be made so that these areas of northern Ontario can be designated as depressed areas, small growth areas, distressed areas or designated areas. Let them be called by any name, but let them receive some assistance instead of being penalized by the attitude of this Government. They should receive treatment at least equal to that afforded other communities which have more advantages.
If the Government took the attitude I suggest it might not cost one red cent because, while I know of no industry which has gone into the designated areas of Timmins or Rouyn, I do know of several industries that will locate in the Timiskaming area when it becomes a designated area so that they can take advantage of that situation. Surely the Minister is fair enough to give the people of Timiskaming the opportunity of having a pulp mill or some other enterprise locate in that area. He can do so by treating them on an equal basis with those people of the areas to be designated.
The program as outlined by the Minister is not fair because the criteria set down by the Department of Labour are not adequate to take into consideration slow growth areas which, a few years ago, grew rather rapidly but then began to deteriorate. I am not suggesting for one minute that this Government should not consider those small towns which exist as a result of the agricultural industry, but I do feel that there has been a
3018	COMMONS
Grants to Designated Areas trend to ignore the rural communities in favour of the urban centres. This has in part led to the urbanization which has taken place in Canada.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
But we are talking about communities with a population of 20,000 which have all the necessary facilities already paid for. In many of these towns that have been built on the mining industry the municipal debt was paid off 10 or 20 years ago. We have the facilities but we do not have the growth and development that other communities have experienced.
We do not want to wait until the situation gets as bad as in the Maritimes. I do not want to represent an area that has died and for which we are trying to bring about some kind of rebirth. I want our area to be given assistance now, so it can continue to participate in the same way as the rest of Ontario. In that regard I would refer to this statement by one Ontario Government department:
The Department of Economics and Development stands ready at all times to help in this development-*
The development of northern Ontario.
-confident that by the proper utilization of our natural and human resources, by faith in the unity of our people, northeastern Ontario can play a most vital role in the fulfilling of Ontario's destiny.
We have helped to maintain Canada in the past. When citizens from every riding in Canada came to the gold mining areas of northern Ontario looking for work they received work and thus were able to maintain their families and help to maintain communities throughout Ontario, Quebec and many other parts of Canada. Now we are asking for equality of opportunity so that we can take advantage of the assistance given to other areas. If we are given this opportunity we will continue to play our part. I can assure hon. Members that there will be no cost to Canada in the end because the contribution we will make will be much greater than any assistance that may be extended to us through this legislation. If this is done we are prepared to support the legislation. If this kind of concession is not made I am prepared to fight the legislation in any way I can until it is made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in listening to the hon. Member for Timiskaming I was reminded of how often, in listening to economic questions being debated at provincial political conventions over the years, I have heard northern Ontario representatives

DEBATES	June 29, 1965
threaten to secede from the Province of Ontario and of how often I have heard eastern Ontario representatives say:	If you are
leaving, for God's sake take us too.
I think the tragedy of the Province of Ontario lies in the fact that development has been centralized in the metropolitan area and in western Ontario and that generally speaking eastern Ontario and northern Ontario have been left as "the poor South" of this great and rich province. In his criticism of the results of the legislation I think there was inherent in the remarks of the hon. Member for Timiskaming the fact that the approach to the economic problems of the nation embodied in this type of legislation is a sound one. What he was complaining about was the fact that the interpretation of the legislation did not suit the particular needs of his people and, in line with his duty as a Member representing these people, he objected in the strongest possible terms to the application of the rules of the legislation. But in principle I think that he and the people of eastern Ontario would agree that the approach of providing a Federal incentive to areas of slow growth, high unemployment and a low rate of growth of employment is a sound one.
This is the first time in the history of this Dominion that this approach has been taken. As we are in many other areas, we in this country have been behind countries such as Italy, the United Kingdom and Sweden with regard to the decentralization of industry.
The hon. Member for Waterloo South said that the emphasis on decentralization should not be negative. In other words, it should not render the economy of the country inefficient in its application. I certainly think that none of us would wish to make Canada's economy inefficient. I take exception and disagree most violently with those ivory tower university economics professors who sit there in their shelter and say that the only way we can be efficient in this nation is to build two or three little Japans from one end of the country to the other, and that this is the only way we can compete in world markets. I say that economists who argue in this fashion negate the entire Canadian challenge. We have a great land mass and a small population and the challenge is: Can we in fact derive the social benefits of that great land mass and still be efficient economically? I think we can do so and I believe that for the first time the Government has recognized that principle by bringing in area development legislation under the Department of Industry.
June 29, 1965

We have not hidden our heads in the sand and said: Let the Japans grow and leave the rest of the land to lie fallow, because in that way we will be efficient. As I said, for the first time the Government of this country has said that this nation should be permitted to grow with some equitable distribution of the sources of production and the sources of employment so that there will not be first and second rate citizens as there are today, and so that we will at least try to minimize the gap between the mountains and the valleys in our economic picture.
I am one of those who disagree with the application of the program in its first stage. I think that the Government deserves credit for bringing in the program and for accepting this philosophy which will lead to the equalization of opportunity across this land, but I do think that we need to become more sophisticated in our approach to the problem. We need to approach it from a proper base and above all we need the courage to approach the problem, if need be, from a basis of common sense, on an ad hoc basis, if you like, on the basis of economic principles, yes, but not on the basis of political patronage at all.
I do not think any set of statistics, no matter how comprehensive they may be, can possibly determine whether a certain area (a) can usefully and economically assimilate industrial growth and (b) whether incentives will contribute to that useful economic growth. I do not think any set of figures, no matter how sophisticated and complex they may be, can provide the perfect answer. In the Ottawa valley there is a saying which I believe has spread throughout a considerable part of the country. It is that "figures don't lie but liars can figure". It may be we need to do a little more figuring in this particular area.
I think the problems of eastern and northern Ontario are similar and unique. I believe we must admit that the statistics and the criteria as they were evolved do injustice to those areas of slow growth in eastern Ontario and northern Ontario. In all fairness I must say that our unemployment picture and our lack of growth of employment are not as critical as in areas such as the Gaspe, part of the eastern townships and a great part of the Maritime Provinces.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words before the motion for second reading is adopted, in order to explain the purposes of the bill to the Members of the House.
The Trustee Board of the Presbyterian Church in Canada was incorporated by chapter 64 of the Statutes of Canada 1939, for the purpose of acquiring, taking and holding and dealing with real and personal property of the church. There was only one amendment, and that was by chapter 23 of the Statutes of Canada 1962-63, which widened the field of investments to include investments in which a Canadian insurance company might invest, and granting power to establish plans for gratuities, pensions, superannuation, etc., for ministers or former ministers of the Presbyterian Church in Canada, and section 23 was added clarifying the references in the Act to the board of administration or the administrative council.
With respect to the purpose of the proposed legislation, at the present time the board consists of seven members established by act of incorporation. It is now desired to make provision for enlarging the number to a maximum of 15, and to provide that until otherwise determined by the general assembly of the church, the board shall consist of eight members.
It has been the practice to appoint the chairman of the administrative council and treasurer of the church to the board. It is desired to make these appointments mandatory, but if the treasurer of the church might at some future time become a permanent paid position, or alternatively might cease to exist under that name, then in either of these two events it is desired to appoint the person holding the position of chairman of the finance committee of the administrative council to the board in place of the treasurer, if that position were not a paid position.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)

In the second place it grants power to combine and consolidate in the hands of the board-to receive the income therefrom and to apportion the net income therefrom pro rata according to the respective interests therein among such

trusts, institutions, organizations, schemes and funds, provided that no such moneys or investments shall be consolidated, if by the terms of the instrument under which they are held they are specifically directed to be administered separately. It also gives power to employ investment counsel or other professional advisers.
In the third place it provides for the enactment and repeal of bylaws, regulations, etc., the power of the general assembly to delegate power and revoke such delegation.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT FOREIGN INTERVENTION IN INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES
MEASURE TO PREVENT FOREIGN INTERVENTION IN INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-12, to amend the Immigration Act (Foreign Intervention in Industrial Disputes).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I hope that bringing this bill before the House will accomplish some of the things which previous bills have done in bringing matters of interest before the House for discussion. It seems, Sir, that from time to time facts are brought to our attention which indicate that there is an ever-increasing American influence on the Canadian way of life. This has been pointed out on several occasions by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), who has endeavoured by legislation and other means to rectify this situation and who has stressed the need to give Canadians the opportunity to buy back their own heritage and their own resources. That is only one aspect of this question; the other concerns the influence of American culture on the Canadian way of life.
We know that by legislation the programming of our national television and radio is restricted to a certain American content in order that Canadian producers and artists are able to make their mark in their own chosen professions. However, Mr. Speaker, there is one aspect of Canadian life which seems to ignore the American influence, and that is in the field of labour and management relations. That is the reason the bill is before the House at this time.
Specifically, the purpose of this bill is to keep Canadian the disputes, negotiations and settlements that occur in Canada between employer and employee, and to prevent

June 29, 1965

foreign fomentation and fermentation of these disputes into test-tube experiments for the benefit of foreign power groups without regard to Canadian employer-employee interests. We have had many instances of foreign participation in our labour relations. As a matter of fact it has been so marked that not so long ago the C.B.C. or some of those who participate in presenting the programs found it advisable to present to the Canadian public a documentary on what happens when there is undue influence brought to bear in a strike in which labour and management are concerned. I refer to the C.B.C. program which caused a great deal of interest several months ago, namely "This Hour has Seven Days", which related to the strike between the Toronto newspapers and the printers.
Here was a situation where we had almost reached agreement between labour and management. However, because of the participation of American strike promoters, who fomented some discord, the strike was kept going; in fact, I believe it is going at the present time. In Canada we have had newspaper strikes where theoretically some of the staff have been on strike for 17 or 20 years. But it takes on a very dangerous aspect when we find that the relations between labour and management are adversely affected by the participation of people from outside this country.
We realize, of course, that there is a very close relationship between Canadian trade unions and those in the United States.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Many of the unions in this country are of the international type with headquarters in the United States. This, of course, is advantageous to Canadian unions in the event of a prolonged strike because they have the benefit of the finances which are enjoyed by unions across the line, making it possible to finance strikes when they go for long periods.
The situation also arises wherein Canadian unions enjoy the support of the international unions when negotiations are carried on and the pension funds are all disbursed from the United States. However, this did not prevent some of the C.B.C. staff from bringing to the attention of the public some of the injustices in this dispute. If we review the script we are caused to wonder why the Canadian public stand idly by and see this type of intervention continuing. It is interesting to examine the
Private Bills
research done by the C.B.C. staff and realize that much of the material which they produced was in fact very factual. The strike in question drew comment from people all across Canada, for the simple reason that it was a strike which neither the publishers nor the union really wanted. But it was a strike which neither the publishers nor the union could afford to lose.
Some classic statements have been made in connection with this strike because it seemed on the verge of settlement so many times. It is interesting to note that those who had done so much research on the topic discovered that three times the officials of the local union No. 91 of the I.T.U. had reached agreement with the newspapers on the issue. However, three times the agreements were rejected by the headquarters of the printers union in Colorado Springs. This, Mr. Speaker, is a sad commentary, because it shows that while we have Canadian labour and management agreed on a settlement, there was this interference and participation by an international union across the line which deprived the newspapers and the others involved of the privilege of reaching a satisfactory settlement.
It is unfortunate that this situation should take place in light of the fact that those involved on this side of the border were quite in agreement as to what should take place. However, the commentary by the C.B.C. investigators went on to say that local 91 struck because its international headquarters in Colorado Springs could not afford to give way to automation, or so it believed.
Again the question could be asked: Why did the Toronto printers strike? Why did they accept the dictation of their U.S. headquarters, turning down three pretty genuine offers from the publishers? One reason, of course, is that the I.T.U. in Colorado Springs controls the pension fund. This is unfortunate because it is the financial aspects of the situation which seem to be the key to the whole problem. This is a challenge, I imagine, to Canadian unions to produce some type of pension plan which will be satisfactory to the membership and make them independent of forces across the border.
It is not only the C.B.C. which was interested in bringing this aspect of Canadian labour and management relations to the attention of the Canadian public. It is more than interesting and timely to note what the Premier of Quebec said about this arrangement between international unions with headquarters across

June 29, 1965
Private Bills
the line and local unions in Canada. He had some difficulty with legislation regarding pension plans which were controlled on the other side of the border. According to the Ottawa Citizen for July 16, 1964 he said:
We cannot touch the international unions. There would be a risk of a general strike of all the locals of the international unions in the province until we gave way...
The great misfortune in Quebec province is that strikes by international union locals can never be settled unless the little local pawns received permission by telephone from their bosses in the United States...
This is the truth. Why bury your head in the sand and refuse to recognize the truth for the truth?
Many of us, Mr. Speaker, have been independent of labour unions and of management, but we feel that the time has come to give some serious study to this whole problem. I do not suppose there is any other country in the world which has its local union with headquarters in a foreign country to the same extent that Canada has. It seems to me that if Canada is going to be able to control its own destiny, promote its own ideas and enjoy its own culture, then something should be done in the not too distant future to make certain that we do achieve a certain amount of independence from our neighbour, friendly though they are. It is for this reason that this bill is brought before this House, simply, as it says in the explanatory note, to keep Canadian those disputes which concern only Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hubert Badanai (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT FOREIGN INTERVENTION IN INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill would amend section 7 of the Immigration Act, which reads as follows:
The following persons may be allowed to enter and remain in Canada as non-immigrants, namely, persons engaged in a legitimate profession or occupation, or who, having entered are in Canada for the temporary exercise of their respective callings.
The hon. Member would add the following:
-no person so engaged shall be allowed to enter Canada or to remain in Canada as a non-immigrant where there is a dispute, collective bargaining, lockout or strike, as defined in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, in the profession, trade or occupation of that person anywhere in Canada.
It seems to me that this is an attempt to use immigration legislation to solve what is essentially a labour problem. From the hon. Member's explanation it seems quite clear that this bill was inspired by the strike against the three Toronto newspapers which began a year ago, and is still unsettled.
[Mr. Ormiston.l
In the course of this strike we allowed the temporary admission or organizers of the International Typographical Union from the United States. Unfortunately this brought about criticism against the three Toronto newspapers involved in the strike as well as some unfavourable comment, on the ground that the American union officials, by their activities and presence in Canada, were prolonging the dispute and preventing a settlement between the publishers and the local union. This is precisely what the hon. Member is trying to convey to the House. At the same time we allowed the admission of a handful of American printers to take on work for the publishers, and this generated more criticism from the union involved.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
Our position in respect of the union organizers is clear enough. The Act provides for the temporary admission of such persons and we would no more be justified in refusing their admission than we would be in refusing the admission of consultants to management or key supervisory personnel coming for a specific purpose and period of time.
Moreover, the Act does not provide us with the authority to refuse the admission of these advisers. This bill is apparently designed to overcome that, although in a statement attributed to the hon. Member, as reported in the Toronto Telegram of April 9, 1965, the bill is intended only to "keep out United States union officials seeking to make trouble in Canadian labour disputes".
Our position in respect of the printers is less clear. They applied for permanent admission to take work with the Toronto publishers and were, in all respects, considered eligible for admission under the terms of the Act and the Regulations. The law makes no provision for the exclusion of an immigrant solely on the ground that his prospective place of employment is not to the liking of government, management or labour.
It may be desirable to have such a provision in immigration law, but it is not there now and as a result we are forced to rely on such grounds as lack of visa or other instruments of admission, if we want to refuse a would-be immigrant who is acceptable on all counts except that he is going to work at some job where a strike is in progress. The Immigration Act provides for refusal on these grounds, but their validity has never been tested in the courts; in any event, they are difficult to justify in the public's eye and are themselves a focal point of criticism.
June 29, 1965

In all these questions the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has tried to maintain a neutral position. We do not hinder the temporary admission of anyone coming in a purely advisory or consultative capacity to labour or management.
Aside from the question of its application to Canadian immigration legislation, the bill has a serious technical defect. It would exclude from Canada any person coming temporarily for any purpose relating to his profession, trade or occupation as long as a labour dispute of any kind existed anywhere in Canada in that person's profession, trade or occupation. This would include technicians coming to repair or service foreign machinery or equipment, administrative personnel, business consultants and professional advisers, whether or not a labour dispute was in progress at the plant or in the area to which they were destined.
There is much to be said on the surface for the proposition that labour-management disputes occurring in Canada, or in the United States for that matter, should be settled in each country without foreign intervention, but a close examination of the facts of industrial life as they have developed over the past 100 years or more does not reveal that this bill can make any contribution to support such a proposition.
There are a large number of transportation operations that run between Canada and the United States, and periodically seniority arrangements compel employees and trade union officials to change their country of residence. In certain circumstances, this bill could prevent such interchange even though there was no connection with a dispute, or collective bargaining, or a strike. There are U.S. rail lines running through southwestern Ontario on which Canadians are employed.
A U.S. railway official could not run into Canada on these lines or on any other rail line running into Canada while a Canadian dispute was in progress, if this bill became law. We would need to station immigration officers in every airport in Canada to turn back air lines personnel, if the international unions they were members of were merely engaged in collective bargaining in Canada.
The hon. Member is mistaken also in supposing that all labour relations advice and guidance that goes both ways across the Canadian and U.S. border through the medium of travelling representatives in "foreign fomentation", would be stopped, as stated in the words of the explanatory note to the bill:
Private Bills
-to prevent foreign fomentation and fermentation of these disputes into test-tube experiments for the benefit of foreign power groups without regard to Canadian employer-employee interests.
Most of this interchange across the border is helpful and constructive and is sought after by employers and trade unions alike, even though for publicity purposes some employers and trade unions in Canada decry the intervention of U.S. unions and companies during disputes. At other times each accepts the fact without question.
Most of the provinces of Canada have somewhat different labour relations and disputes legislation and have mediation services that are designed to deal with disputes. The provisions of this bill would merely add one more complication where enough already exists.
In short, this bill will not achieve its apparent purpose of keeping out of Canada all foreign intervention in Canadian labour troubles. If it is intended to interrupt communication between Canadian and foreign interests during a dispute, a prohibition against the entry of foreign representatives would only be an unfair attitude, since nothing can be done to prevent the exchange of ideas between Canadian and foreign industrial interests and Canadian and foreign labour organizations.
In so far as the actual functions carried out by these representatives are concerned, no doubt persons already in Canada are available, if needed, to perform these functions with the advice and guidance of the foreign interests concerned in the outcome.
I may also add that the immigration White Paper, when presented to Parliament, could result in a complete overhaul of immigration legislation at which time these and all other questions relating to the application of the law would receive the most intensive review to eliminate any deficiencies and inconsistencies which may now exist, and for that reason I would suggest that action on Bill C-I2 be not taken at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am ready to admit that every sovereign nation wants to emphasize its own independence, but with respect to the question of labour unions we have to consider the whole matter on balance, and on balance there is a definite advantage in having international unions. I think I can best illustrate that by this fact. I am not suggesting that the hon. Member for Melville (Mr. Ormiston) is opposed to labour unions, but the basis of a healthy

June 29, 1965
Private Bills
democracy is a strong and independent labour movement. I do not mean by that that an independent labour union must not have its headquarters in the United States or be open to outside influence.
The hon. Member said that he knows of no other country whose labour unions have their headquarters outside the country. We all know that, in Argentina, Peron used the labour movement for the purpose of suppressing the people. I am of the belief that if there had been international labour unions in Argentina which could have influenced the labour movement of that country, or if there had been international labour unions in the Dominican Republic or even in Cuba, we might not have had the spectacle of Peron, Trujillo and Castro because the international unions would have exerted influence on the labour movements in those countries, which would have kept those countries democratic and would not have allowed dictatorships to rise. This is my viewpoint.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT FOREIGN INTERVENTION IN INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES
speechtext: May I ask the hon. Member a question? Were there democratic labour unions in the European countries when they were taken over by dictators?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT FOREIGN INTERVENTION IN INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES
speechtext:
I do not know which countries the hon. Member is referring to. They had labour unions, but they did not have international labour unions which would have given the local unions the strength to oppose dictatorships. This is the point. It was the international labour unions that carried the fight in democratic countries to see to it that dictators did not take over those countries. It is only in countries where the labour movement is strong that democracy is strong.
Labour unions are the foundation and roots of democracy. If a labour union in our country can be given added strength by having the support of a labour union in the United States where international unions were born, then I am all for it, because I am in favour of a strong labour movement in Canada and in every other democratic country in the world.
Let us examine for a moment the facts of industrial life as they exist in Canada and the United States and as they have developed over the last 100 years. I am sure our findings would not reveal any need for such a bill. Let me give another example of why I think it is important to have these connections with international labour unions. Canada and the United States have probably the highest standard of living in the world but it is
[Mr. Klein.l
becoming increasingly more difficult for us to compete in foreign markets with those nations that do not have strong labour movements controlled internationally, because in those countries slave labour can be engaged with the result that they are able to produce more cheaply the same kind of articles that we produce. In addition, the cost of living is much less in those countries. The result is that it is becoming increasingly more difficult for us to compete in foreign markets with countries where labour unions are not strong.
One can only come to the conclusion that the purpose of the bill runs counter to our economic history and geography and that its provisions are unworkable and indeed unenforceable. In essence it may deprive certain individuals of their basic civil liberties even in excess of the rights denied in the famous Sibley immigration case. For example, it is conceivable that disputes, grievance procedures and collective bargaining could be taking place constantly in such a widespread resource as the forest industry. Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to repeat what I said at the outset, that international unions have a place in strengthening democracy and they have a place in maintaining the competitive market that Canada and the United States are so sorely in need of throughout the world.
May I call it seven o'clock.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the House for reverting to motions so I can make a short statement on the matter which I mentioned this afternoon in tabling what is now known as the Dorion report. Normally, Mr. Speaker, after receipt of a report of a royal commission which has been examining matters involving questions of policy or controversy, a government may take some days or even weeks to examine the recommendations or conclusions before having the report publicly released, so that the government at the time of release may give an indication of its own policy in respect of these recommendations or conclusions when that policy has
June 29, 1965

been decided. In the case of the present report, however, it was not submitted to the Government until my return from the Conference of Commonwealth Prime Ministers at 7.40 last night. It was placed before the Cabinet for its information at a meeting at eleven o'clock this morning.
Because of the very great interest in this matter and the degree to which Parliament very properly feels concerned over the conclusions that the Commissioner has reached, the Government felt that the report should be released immediately, and it was for that reason I tabled the report this afternoon. Because of the speed with which action has been taken, the House will understand that the Government has not had an opportunity fully to consider what action it should take with regard to all the conclusions that have been reached by the Commissioner.
Pending this further consideration, after which an announcement will be made, I should like to remind the House at once that the Commissioner in his report has given the opinion that there is prima facie evidence of an offence under the Criminal Code in one case; and conspiracy to obstruct the course of justice in certain others.
The Government has today referred these conclusions to the Deputy Minister of Justice with instructions to examine them at once and advise what action with respect to criminal proceedings should be taken.
There is one other matter arising out of these developments which I wish to announce to the House. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) this morning submitted his resignation to me. After discussing the matter twice with him, I have no course but to advise His Excellency to accept it. I do so with very deep regret.
My hon. friend remains a man and a Minister of unimpeachable integrity-

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext: -and unsullied honour. He is a devoted and unselfish servant of Canada and of his own province. He entered political life only because he was persuaded-and I had something to do with the persuasion- that he could make a contribution to his country's unity and welfare.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext:
I have, therefore, asked him to continue that contribution by considering the acceptance of another post in the administration which would be offered to him. He has written me on this point as
Dorion Commission
follows, and perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I may conclude by reading his letter which I received just a few moments ago:
My Dear Prime Minister:
Since our talk this morning when my offer of resignation was discussed, I have given very serious consideration to your request, supported by our colleagues, that I continue in the Government.
As I have already stated to you, it is my view that the conclusions of the report, as far as I am concerned, are tantamount to no more than a statement on the part of the Commissioner that, had he been in my place, he would have exercised his discretion in a different fashion.
I wish to repeat that my resignation was tendered, not out of a feeling that I had done anything wrong, but because of the feeling that my usefulness as Minister of Justice had been impaired by the situation which has developed.
I need not say how deeply moved I am at the confidence which you, Mr. Prime Minister, and my colleagues have shown me in suggesting that I carry on.
Therefore, while I must insist that my resignation be accepted as Minister of Justice, I would be willing to continue to serve in some other capacity.
May I take this occasion to say how very grateful I am for your kindness and consideration and for your unfailing support during difficult and, at times, even cruel days.
Yours faithfully Guy Favreau.
Mr. Speaker, that is the statement which I wish to make to the House at this time on motions, and after further consideration has been given to the conclusions of the report, as I have said there will be further statements to be made by the Government.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened to the announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) with interest, and I with a degree of personal regret.
One of the concomitants of political life, particularly in the case of Ministers of the Crown, is that those Ministers who are by selection entrusted with the high degree of responsibility which they have to discharge, must discharge that responsibility with an accuracy of judgment and an unimpeachability which can never be questioned.
The administration of departments such as those of-and I select these at random- Fisheries, Industry, Agriculture, perhaps Northern Affairs, do not carry that same high degree of responsibility that the portfolio of Justice does. The government of the day, whichever government it is, cannot expect the continued absolute confidence of the people of this country unless there is that absoluteness of confidence in the administration of justice in Canada.

June 29, 1965
Dorion Commission
One only has to place oneself in the shoes of an ordinary citizen when reading the report of Mr. Justice Dorion to come to the conclusion that serious doubts exist as to the ability of the present Minister to carry on in that portfolio. I find this personally regrettable because I find myself in agreement with the words of the Prime Minister, where he has made reference to the honour and integrity of the Minister concerned. But having said that, the portfolio of Justice is no place for any individual occupying that portfolio to have any lack of judgment such as that which would cast doubt on the administration of justice in Canada.
I think the course the Minister has followed is the only honourable one he could follow, and the course of the Prime Minister in accepting that resignation and making the recommendation to the Governor General that he intends to make, is the only course which he could follow.
The Minister has my commiseration in that I believe his own Prime Minister let him down seriously in the conduct of his responsibilities in the portfolio he occupied.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
The report of Mr. Justice Dorion is nothing less than a serious blot on public life in Canada because it not only affects the Minister of Justice in the manner in which the Prime Minister has expressed, but it affects others in public office. It affects the hon. Member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau), about whom the Commissioner had some very pertinent observations to make, observations which if made in terms of broader terms of reference might have carried more serious consequences indeed in terms of his findings. I imagine this is one of the considerations the Government will have in mind when giving further thought to what should be done.
I take no particular relish-indeed, I take none-in the product of the report of Mr. Justice Dorion. When on November 23, I first raised this matter in the House I did so because I thought it was my responsibility to do so. Members will forgive me if I recall to their minds the comments, not too kindly, from the other side of the House accusing me of a smear, innuendo and MacCarthyism when I was placing these serious matters before hon. Members-matters which have now been given the official sanction of finding by an honoured and able Justice.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext:
It is an emotional moment for me, and it makes me rather sad to think of

the image the administration of justice in this country must have because of the events which have transpired. I cannot refrain from mentioning here the conclusions of Mr. Justice Dorion with respect to Mr. Letendre, who has continued in office throughout the investigation and who, I understand, still continues in office, and whose conduct was described by Mr. Justice Dorion as reprehensible. It seems to me that the least decision the Government could reach, and forthwith, is that Mr. Letendre should be suspended from any further connection with the Department of Justice. He is a gentleman who now has access to secret, top secret and confidential files. Having regard to the conclusions made in regard to him by Mr. Justice Dorion it seems the Government should have made an announcement tonight that the services of this gentleman are terminated forthwith.
I might also express at this moment my personal satisfaction with respect to the findings of Mr. Justice Dorion regarding the conduct of Mr. Lord, conduct which I described on November 23 as that of an innocent dupe. This is borne out by the findings of the Commissioner. I believe the immediate course of the Government in referring the recommendations of the Commissioner with respect to the finding of a prima facie case against certain involved individuals and of the recommendation for the laying of information under the conspiracy sections of the Criminal Code-the reference of these matters to the Deputy Minister of Justice-is one which should have been taken in the first instance. No doubt now that the able and talented officers of the department, have been given the green light to bring their talents to bear on these matters, the appropriate conclusions will be arrived at.
As the Prime Minister has said, between the production of the report at 2.30 and the present moment, very little time has elapsed in which to study these findings. The Official Opposition has had even less time than the Government to consider its ramifications. It is therefore not possible to make recommendations in full as to all the conclusions which have been reached by Mr. Justice Dorion. But no doubt we shall have further observations to make when announcements are made by the Prime Minister on this subject in due course.
My last remaining comment on this whole matter has to do with a question which was introduced into the inquiry by the side door, as it were. It affects one individual who had
June 29, 1965

given 14 years of devoted service to the Government and another who was his assistant in the Indian Affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I speak of Mr. William Grant and Mr. Joseph Armi-shaw. Mr. Grant and his trial have been the subject of editorials in the western press. Mr. Armishaw, I am informed, was acquitted last week of charges of forgery laid against him. I think I can find no better comment to recommend the services of these two devoted civil servants to the administration than that uttered by the Supreme Court Justice who tried both these cases when he said, in the case of Grant: "If I were in Grant's shoes I only wish I had the courage to do as he did."
I urge the Government to reconsider both these cases, since they seem to have been involved with the raising of the matters which gave rise to this inquiry in the first place. I am not attributing any motives whatsoever in this respect, but I suggest to the Government that amends must be made to these civil servants in order that justice may be done.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext:
The report of Chief Justice Dorion which we have just read, or seen, reveals in our opinion a very grave situation, and the Prime Minister has failed so far to discuss in any way the serious implications of the report. I hope that before this part of the session is over we shall be given a detailed account of just what is to be done about this situation.
The fundamental fact is that the Commissioner has accepted the evidence of Mr. Lamontagne that he was offered a bribe of $20,000 by the executive assistant to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in order to influence him to consent to bail for one Rivard, whose extradition was sought by the Government of the United States on narcotics charges. The key sentence of the report is to be found at page 11:
He (Mr. Lamontagne) there met Mr. Denis who offered him a sum of $20,000.00 if he would agree to have Rivard released on bail, pointing out that the Liberal Party would receive a substantial amount should such bail be granted.
Dorion Commission
In other words, to put it plainly, organized international crime was able in Canada, as it has done in so many other parts of the world, to reach into the circles of Government in order to pervert justice with bribery and corruption.
Perhaps the most serious question of all which faces this House is the adequacy of the reaction of those primarily responsible for the administration of justice. The report of the Commission has freed the Minister of Justice from any imputation of personal impropriety. As far as I know, no one has ever suggested there was any personal impropriety on his part. I want to say that many Members of this House, including some on this side, will have heard of his resignation with a great deal of personal regret. We have admired both his courtesy and his integrity.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext:
But, Mr. Speaker, in our opinion it would have been quite impossible for the Minister to have taken any other course than that which he has taken, and quite impossible for the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to have taken any other course than to accept the resignation presented to him. I do not think this would be a proper occasion to go into the points that we might have chosen to make if we had not heard of this resignation tonight. I do not intend to do that. I think one thing has to be pointed out, though, that is not part of this report and which is one of the most extraordinary things, in my view. It is the fact that the hon. Member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau), Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister of Canada, was known by the Minister of Justice to be implicated. Indeed, at one stage the officers of the R.C.M.P. reported that they believed the Member for Dollard to be the kingpin in the whole sorry mess. Although this view was not supported by the evidence, and I notice that it was not found by the Commissioner to be so, the Commissioner has nevertheless found that the hon. Member for Dollard attempted to influence Mr. Lamontagne with a view to securing Rivard's release on bail and this, the Commissioner said, constituted a reprehensible act. The Minister of Justice was fully informed of the details of the involvement of the Member for Dollard, and it appears that not a word was said to the Prime Minister, whose Parliamentary Secretary the Member for Dollard was. We find this failure to be quite incredible. Surely the Minister

June 29, 1965
Dorian Commission
of Justice owed it to his senior colleague to tell him of the implication in a matter of this sort of the Prime Minister's own Parliamentary Secretary, and to tell him promptly and fully.
I do not choose to go into other aspects of the matter at this time, because they are in the report which we have here, and it is not our intention to castigate the Minister in any way-that is out of place at this time. But, Mr. Speaker, it must be remembered that this was no ordinary matter of routine dealing with the criminal law. The allegations involved persons intimately associated with the process of government. An executive assistant such as Mr. Denis was clearly in a position, as confidential adviser and close associate of his Minister, to make important decisions. He appears to have been a young man with many important political connections. Mr. Denis was able to introduce another political associate, one Mr. Masson, to other executive assistants. This associate of Mr. Denis is described by the Commissioner on page 64 of his report as coming into the game perfectly willingly, surmising in all probability that he stood to gain a very substantial reward, and decided to exploit his relationship with Mr. Denis to the full. In these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada and this House are entitled to expect that the Prime Minister will take vigorous and determined action.
The evidence indicates the view of the Commissioner that there was a prima facie case against Mr. Denis of a criminal act, namely the offering of a bribe to obstruct the course of justice. What action is to be taken on that? We would like to hear the answer. The Commissioner's report indicates that the Member for Dollard while a Member of this House was guilty of a reprehensible act which was in conflict with the normal course of justice. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to page 109 of the Commissioner's report, where he is dealing with the memorandum of Inspector Reed of the R.C.M.P. which said:
It would appear Letendre, Lord and Denis were all approached by Mr. Guy Rouleau, M.P., to make representation on behalf of Rivard so the latter could be released on bail. It appears Rouleau's brother may have approached him to see if he (the M.P.) could influence any persons in the Government with respect to the release of Rivard on bail. On the basis of our enquiries to date, we can only show this, and such an approach is not unusual in political circles.
Those words "and such an approach is not unusual in political circles" are underlined

in the report of the Commissioner, quoting Inspector Reed. The Commissioner goes on to make this comment:
If it is true that representations such as those made to Mr. Lamontagne are not exceptional in political circles, it is impossible to admit that when such representations are made with a view to obstruct the course of justice, they should be either permitted or tolerated.
If I may add a comment, Mr. Speaker, I would say that politics is indeed in a sorry state when senior police officers accept as a matter of course that improper political interference may be made in the affairs of the administration of justice.
What action is to be taken, then, in respect of the Member for Dollard? I think we will want to know the answer to this question. The evidence, again, indicates that in the view of the Commissioner a group of witnesses, namely Mrs. Rivard, Eddy Lechasseur, Robert Gignac and Guy Masson, conspired to obstruct the course of justice. What action is to be taken against these people? I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this report will have to be studied very carefully to see whether all is well in the higher levels of the R.C.M.P. It would appear that the Commissioner had serious doubts as to whether the advice apparently given to the Minister of Justice by the Commissioner and Deputy Commissioner of the R.C.M.P. was adequate, or the inquiries as vigorous and effective as they ought to have been.
All in all, Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada will not be satisfied, and this Parliament should not be satisfied, with anything less than full and vigorous action by the Prime Minister in respect of every aspect of this report. The people of Canada will not be satisfied to have the resignation of the Minister of Justice treated as a sort of sacrificial offering which makes it unnecessary to deal further with these matters. The system which produced this unhappy mess requires radical revision.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of our party regret that the Dorion report has brought about the resignation of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) who, by his noble gesture, has recognized that politics does not allow any margin for error. We hope, however, that other members who, in my opinion, are a lot more guilty, will do likewise and I will not hesitate to mention, among others, the chief commissioner of the R.C.M.P. who has
June 29, 1965

made gross mistakes during the inquiry which has produced the report on this scandal. I will not name all the officers under his supervision who would deserve the same fate, but it is easy to suspect all the others who are condemned by the Dorion report.
It seems, when reading this report, that everyone made mistakes in this matter, beginning with the Minister of Justice, including the chief commissioner of the R.C.M.P., down to the guard at the Bordeaux jail.
One can hardly require that human beings never make mistakes and I think that in politics it must be recognized that, in similar circumstances, a mistake results in such disastrous consequences. We are satisfied that charges will be laid against the culprits, against those who committed perjury, against those who performed their duties improperly or exerted undue influence, and we shall wait anxiously for the outcome of those charges.
However, we must point out that the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), who started all this, does not seem very honest by failing to pay tribute to hon. Rene Tremblay who was entirely exonerated from blame. The Dorion report states textually:
Evidence shows that the conduct of Mr. Tremblay is absolutely beyond reproach.
And yet, if I remember rightly, the first attacks were made expressly against that minister who also had the courage to resign when he felt that his reputation was in danger. The hon. Member for Yukon would have been well advised to quote the good words Mr. Justice Dorion had about the people mentioned in this report. Allow me to mention among other things the following conclusion:
The Minister of Justice was justified, at that time, in believing that a charge laid against a person or persons involved would have been difficult to prove before the courts.
I mention this fact because the hon. Member for Yukon himself, when he made those charges, made insinuations; yet he had the same information as the Minister of Justice because he had the same file, and he dared not make charges himself, he simply made innuendos.
I say that because in his conclusions, Justice Dorion complains that his powers were not broad enough. I have personally asked in the house for broader terms of reference for the Dorion royal commission so that it could find out the sources of the hon. Member for Yukon. In my opinion, the administration of justice is quite an important matter and it
Dorion Commission
must be above suspicion at all levels. If we cannot be assured that secret investigations made by the R.C.M.P. will not fall into the hands of anyone at any time I believe that it is of the utmost importance to hold an inquiry as soon as possible to determine where the hon. Member for Yukon got that information.
If such information can cause a minister, a member of parliament or a senior official to resign, then I think the people are entitled to know how the said information, causing such serious damage, leaked. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out since the Dorion inquiry started, newspapers have always had information which the Members of the house did not have and which, today, are found to be true, because they coincide with the conclusions of the Dorion inquiry report.
I think the government should make an investigation in order to find out how such information could be divulged before we knew about it.
In conclusion, I wish to say that we are satisfied with the steps which the government proposes to take in order to correct what has to be corrected.
Following this report I should like to draw to the attention of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the cabinet that the French language is treated in a most revolting way within the R.C.M.P. and that reforms should be undertaken within that organization, considering the attitude taken by its officers toward the French language.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
