Mr. Speaker, first of all, I wish to congratulate Mr. Justice Dorion for his report drafted in an intelligent, impartial, brief and precise manner. I believe Mr. Justice Dorion deserves the congratulations of the house for the manner in which he discharged his duties and prepared the report which is being tabled today.
Then, I would also like to quote an extract from Mr. Justice Dorion's report, on page 137, concerning the Postmaster General (Mr. Tremblay) which states:
Evidence shows that the conduct of Mr. Tremblay is absolutely beyond reproach.
I believe that this deserves to be mentioned, and especially after the numerous innuendoes made in the past in this connection. I should like particularly to refer to the last sentence on this page:

June 29, 1965
Dorion Commission
If Hon. R. Tremblay has suffered consequences from statements or certain published comments, it is to be hoped that the persons responsible will now recognize his honesty and integrity.
Mr. Speaker, I still remember, because it struck me, the question directed to him by the hon. member for Yukon, namely:
"Where were you on the 14th of August, at 8.30"?
That was a bit strong.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON REPORT OF DORION COMMISSION
speechtext: It was dirty.

The former Parliamentary Secretary to the Prfme Minister (Mr. Rouleau), perhaps out of naivety, maybe without full knowledge of the facts or simply in order to do a service to his constituents, did certain things but I am of the opinion that in matters of this kind, one has to be cautious.

constituency over the week end to organize the Liberal party, but that did not bother me too much. However, I was very affected when I learned he had tendered his resignation and that it had been accepted.

He may have acted in this way because he had too many occupations. It has been mentioned that he was the parliamentary leader of his party and party organizer for the province of Quebec. This gave him too much work and he lacked the time to look after everything. Anyway, through an unhappy turn of events, he has handed in his resignation and it has been accepted.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am immensely sorry, as I had a deep liking for the Minister of Justice. I should like to be considered as one of his friends and I deeply regret his resignation.
Mr. Speaker, I would say that he is not necessarily the one who is responsible. Eight or nine months ago-and the Minister of Justice is witness to what I am now saying- indeed, before all this happened, I told him that the R.C.M.P. wanted his head and that they would have it. Mr. Speaker, in reading the findings of this report, one notes everywhere that if the Minister of Justice has acted the way he did, it is because he was ill-advised and ill-directed by the R.C.M.P. Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I had reached the point in the presentation I wish to make to the House where I had commended the Minister and the Government by virtue of the fact that for the first time in the legislative history of this country they have taken pervasive methods to encourage the decentralization of industry or, more specifically in economic terms, to encourage industry to locate in areas of high unemployment and a low rate of growth of employment. At the same time I suggested that it was impossible in one fell swoop to determine criteria which would effectually and perfectly determine which areas (a) could sustain industrial growth usefully and economically and (b) which areas would acquire that industrial growth by virtue of the use of incentives.
In saying this, Mr. Chairman, I do not think I am being in any way critical of the Government's policy in this regard. I think they took a giant step in the first instance. It was not perfection in one fell swoop but certainly it was a giant step in the right direction. It is my hope, as I am sure it is that of all Members who support whole-
June 29, 19SS

heartedly this legislation and the motivations behind it, that as time evolves we will devise a more perfect method of finding the proper areas which should receive incentives and thus contribute not only to the growth of those areas but to the general health of the Canadian economy.
I would point out that the hon. Member for Wellington South, who spoke for the Official Opposition on this matter, spoke with a forked tongue as the Official Opposition so often does. I wrote down his words verbatim, I believe. I understand he is the official spokesman for the Official Opposition on matters of industry. At one stage he said, "We are in favour of the principle of this legislation", but with the other side of his tongue he said, "We are against grants". He also said they are against the federal Government entering this field and that it should be left to the municipalities and provinces.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
I do not know whether he is for or against. He is walking up both sides of the road at once, but I think the position of the Official Opposition in this regard should be made crystal clear. Unless it is refuted by some higher authority than the alleged official spokesman, the hon. Member for Wellington South, then the people of Canada, and of Ontario in particular, can take it that the Official Opposition is against this type of legislation which will lead to the decentralization of industry.
I take it that the hon. Member for Wellington South has put his party on record as being for the continuation of centralization of industry in Ontario and in the Dominion generally. Such being the case, we see here a very distinct division between the Government and the Official Opposition, because through these policies we are clearly on record as favouring the decentralization of industry and the location of industry in designated depressed areas.
Another spokesman for the Official Opposition, the hon. Member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot mumbled something about patronage and political motivation behind this legislation. Mr. Chairman, this is another area where the Official Opposition, in their ill-fated days in office, timidly dunked their toes into the waters of potential decentralization of industry, but apart from a lot of political jargon and big talk, accomplished very little.
I would point out that the very limited incentives they provided, which incidentally proved just as ineffective as their administra-

There were no specific criteria that the government of that day used in propounding the depressed area formula. It was purely and simply a Cabinet decision. I can think of no more effective pork barrel than that, that the Cabinet in its great wisdom-and Lord knows it had little in those days-could decide what areas qualified. If the government of that day decided that a particular community or a particular application merited designation, then for any reason it pleased it could designate that area for double depreciation. If that is not good, practical, pragmatic politics I do not know what is, because obviously it could make the designation purely and simply by reason of the fact that some good Tories had applied for designation. There were no rules, so let us not have the hon. Member for St. Hya-cinthe-Bagot get up on his high horse and talk about political motivation and political practices in this legislation. The legislation his government passed was pragmatically political, but unfortunately so ill-conceived that it was of no earthly use.
I commend the present Government for using economic motivations in the legislation it has presented. The hon. Member for Wellington South takes umbrage at the fact that this legislation in some fashion resembles legislation passed south of the border. Well, Mr. Chairman, if it is in the best interests of the people of Canada, and specifically in the best interests of my constituents, I do not care whether it resembles legislation passed in Mozambique. I am very pleased to have it on the legislative record of this Government.
Maybe the hon. Member for Wellington South has not heard, but if I listened correctly to the views of the Leader of the Opposition on the Viet Nam crisis, he is now solidly proAmerican. Maybe the hon. Member has not kept up with the gyrations of his leader on this issue. It seems communications over there
June 29, 1965

Grants to Designated Areas are not too good, and the hon. Member for Wellington South is still anti-American in his economic views, even though his leader is now strongly pro-American in his views on foreign affairs. I reiterate that so far as I am concerned I do not think it matters who thought of it first. The only question should be, is it in the best interests of our people?
Again the hon. Member for Wellington South raises the old bogey of encroachment upon private enterprise. What a sacred Tory song this has been over the years. It is the same song the traditional Tories raised when children were taken out of the coal mines. They said it was an encroachment upon private enterprise, and it seems to me when they abolished capital punishment for stealing a loaf of bread or a shilling, the good old Tories said, "My goodness, what an encroachment on private enterprise." It is nice to see that the hon. Member for Wellington South, their official spokesman in the sophisticated area of industry, is still singing that same old Tory song, that it is an encroachment on private enterprise.
If this legislation will contribute to the equalization of economic opportunities across this land, if it will mean there will be far less of second class citizens economically across this land, whereby second class citizens have less social and educational opportunity, then if it is an encroachment upon private enterprise it is a proper encroachment upon it.
It has been the history of this party that we have been able to choose and to discriminate between improper encroachments and encroachments which were in the public interest. For that reason, over the years since the industrial revolution, this party has had the support not only of the people generally but of those who believe in the private system of economic production.
I would like to speak for a moment on the question of the selection of the areas to be chosen for these incentives. I have said as forcibly as I can that the general aim and purpose of the legislation are admirable. Surely anyone who has been in these unfortunate areas, which have not shared in the growth of this land, cannot doubt that legislation of this type was badly needed. I have seen areas in this land, some in my own constituency, where wages were as low as 85 cents an hour within the last two years. This may be inconceivable to those who live in the great golden horseshoe of the metropolitan area in this province, but it is a fact.


I have seen many areas where, because of lack of assessment, children up to the age of entering high school were in one room, from kindergarten right up, and under one teacher. Surely to goodness, in a land that last year had the second highest per capita income in the world, this is not good enough. I have seen areas where there is no high school and no possibility of children going to high school because the assessment would not support a high school.

I should not have to say more.

It would be the height of folly to locate industry by offering financial incentives in a place where it would perish after the incentives had been withdrawn. I thank the hon. Member for Ontario for his courtesy. I will not be too long.
June 29, 1965	COMMONS
The original criteria certainly did the job to some extent, and the legislation marked a bold first step. It is my hope, with the experience the officials of the department have had, that a more meaningful set of criteria can be developed, criteria which will make it possible for smaller pockets which are currently lagging behind the general economic development of a province, to make economic progress.
A new theory with respect to these incentives may be brought into being at this time.
I agree it is almost impossible to find a set of criteria to provide a perfect answer. But I do believe there should be some distinction, and I will make my point in this way: In the area I have the honour to represent and, in particular, in the great part of the constituency of South Renfrew there used to be a prosperous and economically sound lumbering industry. It has now been largely cleared. The people living there are able. They are self-sufficient, or they would not have survived for as long as they have. They do not have the highly sophisticated skills which are required in the metropolitan centres today, but there is no question about their ability to support useful economic growth. Industries which located there in the past have proved to be among the most efficient, the most productive and the most lasting in our entire economy. The productivity of these people has been proved.
While the over-all problem is the problem applicable to great areas such as the Maritime Provinces, the difficulty is to find a set of standards in a generally rich province such as Ontario which will be applicable to those small pockets where help is so badly needed. I do not look upon this as a handout. Consider the hundreds of millions we are pouring into urban redevelopment in the great metropolitan cities to remedy the problems created by growth over the years. Communications in these centres cost a great deal-subways, highways, throughways on top of all this. And soon we will need parachutes to ride on the top layer of the highways. A lot of public money is being spent in these areas.
In the area I speak of, our natural resources have been exploited; not manufactured on the spot but removed for use and manufacture in the metropolitan centres. Water resources, the natural asset of these people, have been taken away for use in the large metropolitan cities, and hydro rates are far higher near the sources of power than they
DEBATES	3035
Grants to Designated Areas are in the metropolis itself. I uo not think these people are looking for handouts; they are looking for economic justice. I grant that the brigands-I am talking about the removal of hydro and natural resources-were not federal brigands but provincial brigands. More enlightened provinces provided for processing at the source, but in this case it was the province which took away from these people the natural assets which the good Lord had given them. I think it is a fine thing that the federal Government has seen fit to take steps which would give some measure of economic justice to these areas and, as I have said before, it may be that as a result of their experience the departmental officials will be able to work out a formula whereby designation might be made of these large areas which obviously need assistance, while at the same time being flexible enough to provide assistance in areas of the Ottawa Valley and similar areas which, possibly, are in no need of the long term aid which is required in the case of the Mari-times.
Many of us have worked for years to encourage industry to take root in the area of which I speak. Competition for industrial development is keen, today. The difference between an area getting an industry and not getting one can be very slight. A nudge will decide the issue one way or another. These capital grants are likely to prove an effective incentive. And, of course, of what use are incentives unless they are effective? There is little point in providing incentives, such as double depreciation allowances, if industry is not interested in them. But even when incentives were far less effective than they are now likely to be, areas such as those I have in mind found it difficult to attract new industries in competition with those to which some assistance was provided. If they are placed further behind, because other industries will get grants while they cannot, they will be condemned for all times to be second class citizens, and I am sure the Government would not wish this to happen.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
In the Ottawa Valley and in the west end of the riding of South Renfrew, of which I speak in particular, I think the natural growth centre is the Town of Renfrew. This is within 30 miles of most of the highly depressed area. Industry locating there will bring people from this area of unemployment and slow growth into that town for employment. Three or four industries in this area would solve all the
June 29, 1965

Grants to Designated Areas problems. Therefore it may be that these programs can be approached differently and made more flexible in areas such as the Mari-times as compared with these smaller pockets of slow growth in provinces such as Ontario.
It is my hope and purpose in speaking on this measure at this time to urge the departmental officials to see if they cannot work out criteria that will be effective in the broad sense in areas where there are large land masses which need progress, but which will also be applicable in a different sense, if you like, in areas such as the generally wealthy Province of Ontario where small pockets have fallen behind in the general growth prosperity which is to be found across most parts of this land.
May I again commend the Minister, his officials and this Government for this far-seeing and I think highly progressive measure, and may I on behalf of the constituents who sent me here plead that they find methods and criteria whereby these plans may be made applicable to smaller areas of slow growth such as exist in the Province of Ontario.
Mr. Winkler? Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to follow the hon. Member for Ren-few South. He sounded this evening as though he were preaching for a call. I do not know whether there will be something available for him, but he has preached for that call before and has not been very successful. It may be that he has been accepted on a greater and wider basis by the Government than I would think to be the case. I am also very pleased that he was able to take advantage of the request of the Opposition to continue his speech beyond the time allotted, because I believe it was the Government who wanted to streamline the business of the House by eliminating or reducing speeches on different stages of measures brought before the House. However, Mr. Chairman, that being the case we will carry on with some of the arguments the hon. Member put forth and I will then advance some thoughts of my own.
I must admit that I found some of the points made by the hon. Member acceptable, and I have some area of agreement with them. But when he castigates the Conservative Party when in power for their failure to deal with the situation on the tax incentive basis in regard to write-offs, I must say that he was castigating us on the basis of our considering the whole matter from the point of view of slow growth. Then later on in his address he pointed out vehemently that this is the


way it must be considered and one of the points in the criteria that must be taken into account is the growth rate of the different communities particularly, as he pointed out, in the Province of Ontario. So we have, again, the hon. Member for Renfrew South creating quite a paradox in the course of his speech. It seems that he is putting his argument across quite sensibly until you examine his words.
I also listened to him as he developed his argument with regard to the failure of the Conservative Government in this connection. I can recall very well, not too many years ago, in the light of what has happened in this House this evening, the present Prime Minister demanding that the Government resign and pass the reins of government over to his party. Unless the Government is prepared to meet some of the requests made by the hon. Member for Renfrew South and some other Members in this House, who know what this legislation will mean if properly applied, I think the day is here when the Liberal Party should consider passing the reins of office back over here where they properly belong.

I wonder whether the hon. Member would call that patronage. Is that a bit unfair? Is that a bit of the pork-barrel stuff? We know very well where these Members get their financial support from. In view of this, Mr. Chairman, the hon. Member should look at his words this evening. I think it is high time that he recognized who is responsible for this situation. He was speaking out of both sides of his mouth; he was congratulating the Minister for having come

forward with this measure, and he was stating what in his opinion should be the criteria applied to it. What is he going to say if the criteria applied are not what he wants? He will stand up, like every other Grit on that side of the House, and vote for the measure. That is exactly what will happen. This is the course of events that his party has foDowed, and he will act no differently in this particular case. We do not criticize this legislation too severely if it is carried out in these terms in the bill, and the Government acts with common sense, because then this program will be implemented effectively and fairly across this country.
No reference has been made with regard to the position of the more wealthy provinces in this country in relation to those who want a more equitable share of the growth that has taken place and is about to take place.
I have no argument on that particular point, because I think everyone in this House knows that the Maritime Provinces are one area of this country that need support and should receive special consideration. I also think that because of the past history of the Province of Saskatchewan this is another area which should be considered, because we know the growth rate of the population and the trends, and so on, which have taken place there in the past. This province, too, should be eligible for a considerable degree of consideration when the criteria are set up and the designations are being made.
If we read all the words contained in the resolution that is under discussion at the present time I do not think anyone in this House would wish to argue about the points that are promoted in it. With regard to the actual implementation of the legislation, we believe that this is the area in which the Government should move to bring about the fulfilment of the ideas that are our interpretation of what is required, and what in actual fact should be done. I would refer at this moment, Mr. Chairman, to the words of the Prime Minister on June 7, as reported on page 2023 of Hansard, when he referred to this matter. These words are to be found in the left-hand column, and the Prime Minister put it this way:
The purpose of this program is to provide a broad improvement in the incentives to industrial development-
He also uses the word "underemployment" in another context, although I believe these purposes may be associated. Then he went on to say this:

Grants to Designated Areas There are many more specific measures that can assist industrial development, and provincial governments are developing such measures in regional development plans within their provinces.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I believe that the thoughts expressed by the Prime Minister at that time are good ones. This is one way in which the Government can satisfy the needs of the provinces, even the needs of the Province of Ontario.
Long have I felt that there should be some method of redistributing the industrial wealth of this nation in such a way that, where practicable, some measure of growth and development can sensibly take place. We know the Government has been very effective at redistribution in another sense and, although as I have said on other occasions, this does not particularly bother me, I do want to make my point before it is too late. An area such as the one from which I come, for example, could use such support, and the Minister knows full well the importance of my words and what is meant by them, though I will elaborate in a moment.
Nevertheless, we find ourselves being redistributed politically so that our voice will become considerably less in this House. Yet we have found in the past that there has been no activity on the part of the Government to redistribute some of the wealth of the people who have seen fit to stay in that part of the country, wealth which has increased at the rate which has been established, particularly since World War II. I believe that as the natural resources of North America are depleted, particularly in the area south of us, then unquestionably the trend economically and industrially will, I believe, in due course be to the north, and thus of great advantage to Canada.
In order to make a proper plan I believe that the terms of such a resolution as this and the legislation to follow can effectively be used to this end. I believe that as we sit here representing this great country of Canada from one sea to the other sea, tremendous opportunities for development will appear if the benefits and incentives which will be created from this legislation are properly and sensibly applied.
Let me return again, Mr. Chairman, to my own constituency. In this regard I should like to refer to the Ontario Statistical Review, which is available to anyone who wishes to consult it. The figures found therein are rather important. They would indicate that the Minister and his officials would find
June 29, 1965

Grants to Designated Areas the report useful in considering the criteria for the designation of the areas he intends to establish. I am aware, Mr. Chairman, that the County of Bruce, which is an area into which I have presently been moved rather forcibly, is one of these areas. The County of Grey, in which I actually live, is also one of these areas. You will find generally, Mr. Chairman, that all the counties in the vicinity of Georgian Bay made strong representations to the Minister, before this legislation was introduced, to be considered under the terms of this new legislation. I will have to read a few words from this resolution to make my point clear. The resolution is:
That It is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the payment of development grants to assist the establishment of new manufacturing or processing facilities and the expansion of existing manufacturing or processing facilities in order to improve industrial employment opportunities in designated areas in Canada;-
Then it goes on to mention the amount of money to be credited to the area development account in the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
I would take it that in using the words "to improve industrial employment opportunities" the Minister is referring to those areas which need these opportunities and which would benefit the most from them. Inasmuch as the counties to which I have made reference are usually considered rural counties, and on the basis of the facts and figures placed before the Minister and the representations made to him some time ago, I believe that my county is one deserving consideration.
I have before me the percentage figures of change in the County of Bruce from 1951 to 1961. For the County of Bruce it is 4.2 per cent, and it rates 51st out of the 53 areas selected in the Province of Ontario. The figures for Grey County in this same regard are 5.2 per cent, rating 50th in the province

out of 53 such areas. The next set of figures indicate, as the hon. Member for Renfrew South was obviously aware, that young people seeking the advantages which exist in the larger and more prosperous areas in the Province of Ontario to the south of us leave their homes and communities in order to participate in the economic advantages open to them. The figures indicate that 31.5 per cent of persons between 20 and 49 years of age, living in the County of Bruce in 1961, expressed as a percentage of the population, fell into the above category, the county ranking 51st out of the 53 areas. The figure for Grey County is 33.6 per cent, ranking 44th.
There are also other figures in this review, for example relating to incomes, which are important to the Minister in considering the areas to be designated and which back up my request, and the request of the people who have been in touch with him, to consider the entire Georgian Bay development area as a designated area.
Although this is not contained in the report, I became aware early this spring, when the income picture of the farmers in these areas became critical, that the agricultural office in the Village of Markdale had conducted a survey to find out what was the net return of a selected group of ten farmers. I was absolutely amazed to find that six out of the ten showed a minus net return. Therefore it is easy to see why the young people in the families occupying these farms will not be able to continue on in occupation very long, unless the Government extends the provisions of such legislation as this to the areas I have mentioned.
I do not want my words to prejudice to any degree the communities to which I have referred. I ask the Minister to do nothing more than give further consideration to the areas, and to any area in the entire Dominion of Canada which finds itself in this situation. We certainly do not hold this particular case in abhorrence, but we are afraid that in the final analysis the Government will return to the old form, under which certain areas will receive a thumbs-down treatment, for various reasons. I should not want the Government generally or the hon. Member for Renfrew South specifically to think for one moment that anyone on this side of the House is in support, to any degree, of centralization as opposed to the benefits which may flow from this legislation. The hon. Member for Renfrew South again used his ability to twist the words to suit his own purposes and, I might add,

that is characteristic of his attitude and the attitude of his colleagues.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
We have no argument against benefits which might flow from this legislation to those areas where an economic advantage exists. However, the hon. Member does not have to deride the educational system now in existence in Ontario because, as he is well aware, it is a very excellent system and is improving rapidly in excellence in our rural areas. I might add that this is the direct result of many of the policies adopted and forwarded by the hon. Member for Ontario when he was the Minister of Labour.
If we use the advantages inherent in this legislation and direct industries, which we know would be of benefit to certain communities, to establish in a location, a great deal of benefit will be gained, and I am sure this is true of the two counties to which I have referred. The hon. Member for Grey North will agree with me in this regard. With the advent of the St. Lawrence Seaway, tremendous economic advantages were lost to the people of the surrounding areas, and particularly the area in the neighbourhood of Owen Sound.
Mr. Chairman, we are particularly anxious to support this legislation, provided we are given some assurance that it will be administered properly and in a way advantageous to the people of the areas affected, and to the people of Canada as a whole. There are certain economic advantages which can be gained as a result of the adoption of this measure, but there are inherent dangers which must be avoided. Having regard to certain market areas of southern Ontario and the incentive provided industry to locate there, let me assure the House and the Minister that we will take advantage of any benefits provided by this legislation in order that the sorely needed industry will locate there. I am sure the people of the area will work endlessly toward this goal.
I urge the Government and the Minister once again to give serious consideration to the terms of this legislation and the economic effects inherent in it. I hope that due consideration will be given to a review of the circumstances which exist in those areas which may well benefit from a proper administration of this plan.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was very interested this afternoon, as I am sure all hon. Members were, to hear the
DEBATES	3039
Grants to Designated Areas very unusual and interesting speech of the hon. Member for Renfrew South. Of the 35 minutes during which he spoke on this subject, and I was pleased that he was given an extra 15 minutes over and above the allocated time for speeches at this stage of the legislation, he spent 20 minutes pointing out that the problems of this country have arisen during the last 97 years of Liberal and Conservative Governments. It is true that he jumped back and forth from one subject to another, but he placed special emphasis on that fact. He spoke extensively about the difficulties which now face the people who live in the valley which he represents, that valley which 100 years ago was one of the most beautiful places the people of the world have ever seen. Unfortunately that area does not look so beautiful today. The hon. Member spoke of water pollution, and other associated problems, and the possible solution to those difficulties.
To make a long story short, I am pleased that a Member on the Government side has finally realized and recognized the problems this country is faced with today. He devoted his first 20 minutes to a discussion of these problems, and possible solutions. However, in the final 15 minutes he attempted to defend this measure as a complete solution to these problems. I am afraid that this measure will provide no more of a solution to these problems than the measure adopted by this Government not too long ago. Incidentally, the Conservative Government also adopted a program which, to all intents and purposes, was to solve these problems but, like the Liberal Government, it had to be dropped as a failure. It is our feeling that this measure will likewise prove to be completely insufficient as a solution to our present day difficulties.
The hon. Member mentioned also that this measure would work toward decentralization of industry and help solve some of our growth problems of today. In view of the fact that the trend today is for young people to leave small communities and farming areas to go to the more populous areas of Canada to seek employment, I am wondering whether this measure will help to decentralize industry, or will in turn attract the young people from our rural areas to these designated areas and in effect worsen the situation. That seems to be one of the fundamental weaknesses of this measure. That was also a fundamental weakness of a similar proposal which was presented to this House some years ago.
June 29, 1965

Grants to Designated Areas
In view of past experiences of governments in efforts to designate areas and decentralize industry, I believe the Minister and his Government should now take a long look at this proposal. I am sure if they do so they will realize that this is the wrong approach. They should take a thorough look at the problems which now face thousands of people in this country, before adopting any policy of this kind. The employment situation in this country is becoming worse and worse every day, and sooner or later the Government will have to adopt sound policy.
At this time I should like to take the opportunity of pointing out some of the dangers inherent in the presently proposed scheme. I feel that I am in a position to talk about these dangers because of my experience, coming from a designated area. The area from which I come was designated two years ago. Immediately prior to its designation a meeting was held, at which a great deal of enthusiasm was developed for the then proposed plan.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
But when all the interested people who were gathered there started to examine the matter a little more closely there was not one single application made under that scheme. So it just did not fit the bill.
There is another reason I feel qualified to speak on this particular subject and to point out the dangers inherent in it. Ever since the big mineral strike in the Timmins area last year, ugly rumours have been floating about that certain other areas of Ontario are out to try to steal the Timmins smelter. One area mentioned in this regard is the constituency of the Prime Minister. Having this in mind, it is no wonder that we look at this particular scheme with a great deal of apprehension and suspicion.
We have not seen the bill, but judging from what I have heard so far all of the present designated areas will become undesignated as of the 1st of July-I hope the Minister will correct me if I am wrong-and effective immediately on that date we will have a whole new group of designated areas. Some of them may be the same, some may be new and some of the old ones will be dropped. In view of the rumour that has been raising its ugly head from time to time in the Timmins area, how easy it would be for the Government under this scheme to arrange to remove the Timmins area from the designated list and to designate the Elliot Lake area. It is true that

someone could go ahead and build a smelter in Timmins, but they would be faced with competition from a smelter built in the other area, with regard to which federal taxpayers would be paying 22J per cent of the cost. This is one of the reasons we are looking at this matter very closely. The people of the Timmins area are fully aware that if things are decided on a purely economic basis the only sane and sensible place for the smelter to be built is in the Timmins area and that if it is built anywhere else it will be because of either political or financial pressure.
Some hon. Members may think that the hon. Member for Timiskaming was rather brash this afternoon when he spoke about the temper of the people of the north, but I should like to assure the House that he was not. Feelings are running very deeply in that area. The people of northeastern Ontario are sick and tired of being the milk cow not only for the Province of Ontario but for the whole North American continent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF DEVELOPMENT GRANTS IN DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister advanced some interesting arguments as to why this kind of program would be more effective to deal with areas of unemployment than the plan initiated last year respecting designated areas. I agree with his contention that it will be easier to expand employment opportunities in an area when direct cash
June 29. 1965

Grants to Designated Areas grants can be made available for the establishment of new industry. I also agree with him that there is a problem in achieving industrial expansion on the basis of income tax or corporation tax holidays, or accelerated depreciation, when it is necessary for industries to earn an income, shortly after their establishment, which would be taxable. Many types of industry require several years to become established and reach the point of substantial income that can be used for accelerated write-off or tax holidays.
Notwithstanding that those arguments are valid, I want it to be abundantly clear I am generally opposed to the kind of program envisaged in this resolution, and for that matter to the kind of government action taken under the old designated area type of assistance. I say so because I am reasonably sure that under the old program some industrial establishments were misplaced so far as economic soundness is concerned, particularly after the expiration of the incentive period, and 1 feel this program of direct cash grants from the federal treasury will have the same effect. When industries established under it come face to face with the economic realities of competing without incentives, they will find themselves unable to carry on because of location.
This is more detrimental to the communities involved than if no industries had been established in the first place. In other words, what I am saying is that if a new industry establishes in an area and employs X number of employees, it places a great load on the municipality concerned, to provide for those people when the industry can no longer compete without incentives. This is something which will have to be carefully considered, else there will be many groups of people who will find their jobs in jeopardy at the expiration of the incentive period.
We shall then be faced with two alternatives, having to continue to subsidize these industries where it is uneconomically feasible for them to compete, or else having the municipalities support the unemployed workers, should they close down. I do not believe that we can assist the weak by pulling down the strong. If we take the tax dollars we collect from the strong economic sectors of our country, and use them to set up industries in competition with the industries providing those tax dollars, it will be a very serious matter and one we need to consider carefully.
At present there is a redistribution taking place of the corporation and income taxes

coming into the federal Government and going out to the provinces by way of grants and the equalization formula. This provides a distribution of tax income to those areas lagging behind the more buoyant sectors of the country. Further, provision is made by certain provinces to attract industry to them through tax concessions and other incentives. The provincial governments are using the additional funds made available to them by the federal Government to provide these incentives, but I do not think anyone objects particularly to that.
We are a nation of many regions, and we are our brother's keeper to a point-to the point that we should provide some inducement to areas that are lagging behind, enabling them to catch up and maintain a decent standard of living. But you reach a point of diminishing returns in this matter of establishing industries in areas where they cannot compete without subsidization. The Government ought to be very careful in penalizing the prosperous areas through additional taxation in order to establish uneconomically feasible misplaced industrial establishments in other areas.
If the Government is going to go ahead with this kind of program it should be very careful to take into account the criteria that will be used to designate a development area. We are informed that there will be such things in the formula as the level of income, and factors respecting low employment opportunities, low growth opportunities, and things like that. I do not disagree with these factors being introduced, but I notice there is an addition to what were the criteria when designated areas were first established.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
But the income levels should be considered together with the cost of living in the local national employment service area. To reach the same standard of living in different areas may require a different level of income. Compare the cost of living in Toronto with the cost of living in some areas in Saskatchewan or the Maritimes or even in certain parts of Alberta. We would find that the cost of living in Toronto is substantially higher. What we should be concerned with is the standard of living. These two factors are closely related.
Perhaps by way of experiment we could vote $50 million to see what effect it has. But we should not go too far. If this goes further and further, the Government will get into the business of attracting industry by way of offering incentives, as some of the provinces
June 29, 1965

have already done. We are going to get into the rat-race where every province tries to outbid the other in attracting industry. We have already had experience of this-municipal governments outbidding their neighbours in offering tax concessions and the like. The point will be reached where some of the richer provinces will be forced in self-defence to set up incentive and concession programs. Then where does the balance go? The Province of Alberta has made its position very clear. It has been trying to resist this kind of Government intervention, this method of attracting industry by offering subsidies. If Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and, now, the federal Government, insist on using public funds to attract industries into areas other than Alberta, then I think Alberta will find it necessary in self-defence to use the vast resources and reserves of that province to set up its own incentive program. Then we would find ourselves in a position where one offer of incentives balanced out the other. At this point, I suggest, some of the richer provinces, which are in a far stronger position to offer incentives, would be forced to do so. I hope the Minister will be careful to see that a program of this kind does not discourage the natural location of industries, which because of sound economic reasons place themselves in proximity to markets and raw materials, natural advantages enabling them to build up enterprises capable of continuing in the face of competition, without need for incentives. If we go too far in the direction now proposed we shall weaken the whole economic structure of the nation and I am sure the Minister would agree that this is not desirable.

speechtext:
I have a few remarks to make on the resolution stage of the bill which the Minister will be presenting in due course. I hope the hon. gentleman will present the bill at an early date so that we may study its contents carefully and be in a position to go into full detail.
I listened with interest to what the hon. gentleman had to say. If I understood him correctly he told us that the benefits so far, tax concessions and accelerated depreciation allowances, have been limited benefits only.
I do not intend to repeat what I said during the budget debate. It is on record in Hansard. Some hon. Members like to go back to these things, but I would prefer to let the record speak for itself. At that time I said I did not believe the tax concessions, or the accelerated depreciation allowances,

Grants to Designated Areas were sufficient incentive to induce industry to go to the designated areas. It has been suggested that two new plants in my own area, the Scott Paper Company and the Clairtone Company were put there as a result of the incentives offered by the Government. It has been maintained that the Scott Company will perhaps gain some $14 million as a result of these income tax concessions. This was suggested in the press. Clairtone, it was said, would benefit by a couple of million dollars. However, I think these figures can only be an approximation as both companies must make a profit in the first three years. These firms have not yet set up their plants; they are just getting into operation. We are happy to have them with us, but the amounts which have been mentioned can only be approximations, even though apparently, they were given to the press. I think they are on the optimistic side, because these plants must make a profit in the first three years in order to gain any benefit.
I am glad the Minister is bringing forward this bill which will provide for assistance to the designated areas. While speaking in the budget debate I mentioned a submission by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council to the Atlantic Development Board setting out what the council felt should be brought forward. I know the Minister has studied these submissions before submitting the resolution and the bill which is to come, because the resolution has some of the features which were recommended by APEC to the Atlantic Development Board. I hope these proposals will be of benefit to the designated areas.
It has been suggested that existing industries can benefit by this legislation. The criterion seems to be that they should contribute appreciably to employment in the area-that is, their extension. I hope the Minister will spell this out clearly in the legislation because a clear definition would be appreciated. I think especially of one industry in my area, the Trenton plants, the biggest employer in the constituency, where formerly as was pointed out to me the existing industry could derive no benefit from the former legislation. I hope the provision now proposed is not a meaningless one and that the criteria set out in the Prime Minister's original statement will not be so narrow as to prevent assistance being given to established industries such as I have mentioned.
June 29. 1965

Grants to Designated Areas [DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
When the hon. Member for Wellington South spoke earlier today he urged that some safeguard should be attached to these grants. I agree with him. The Department of Industry should look into this matter and when making these grants it should satisfy itself that the industry which is to benefit is not likely to be a fly-by-night concern. An industry which set up in an area, took advantage of all the benefits it could receive from federal, provincial and municipal levels and then took off suddenly, would do an area more harm than good. I think there should definitely be very strong safeguards in the matter of grants before they are given to any industry.
Mention was also made by the Prime Minister, on page 3 of the statement which he originally gave, of the following:
The purpose of this program is to provide a broad improvement in the incentives to industrial development in those parts of the country where underemployment is most serious. There are many more specific measures that can assist industrial development and provincial governments are developing such measures in regional development plans within their provinces.
Then he said:
As those plans are elaborated it will be the Government's policy to seek the fullest harmonization between its action and provincial programs.
I would hope that the Prime Minister means that this program will go along, as he stated, in seeking the fullest harmonization between the action of the Government and provincial programs. I am thinking especially of the Province of Nova Scotia and Industrial Estates, a Crown corporation set up by the present provincial government to get industry into the area. Suggestions have been made through the years that the Atlantic Development Board, which was set up by the former government and continued by this one, should give funds to Industrial Estates to help them in their work. I know, going back a few years to when Industrial Estates was but an infant, that there were difficulties in the work of this organization. I spoke to an official and one of the businessmen of Industrial Estates, who is still in that capacity, and he said, "We have so much money to induce industry to come to Nova Scotia, but there are certain things which are just a little beyond our ability because they are just too costly for us to look after. We believe there should be federal help in this regard".
Suggestions were made that the Atlantic Development Board should funnel some of
IMr. MacEwan.]
their funds into bodies such as Industrial Estates. I hope the announcement of the Prime Minister means that in this bill the Government will come forward with some method of achieving the fullest harmonization with Industrial Estates of Nova Scotia. I think this measure could do a great deal for that Province and indeed for the whole Atlantic area. I believe that New Brunswick has set up a Crown corporation, something along the lines of the corporation set up by the Province of Nova Scotia, and I hope New Brunswick will be successful in this regard. But I do hope that the bill brought forward by the Minister will point out in detail how this harmonization can be achieved.
Other Members have spoken on this measure. We will have to get the bill before us, of course, to understand its details in full. However, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could point out briefly that suggestions have been made, one of which is that subsidies should not be provided to industry and should not be given for an indefinite period. I agree with that argument. I believe that subsidies should be on a temporary, interim basis to give a chance to an industry to get on its feet, and from there on it should be able to handle its affairs. The grants should be going to industries which, as I said originally, are set up by substantial companies and which will remain in the area and make a home in which they can settle.
The hon. Member for Renfrew South spoke this evening. I am always glad to hear him. I do not intend to enter into a debate on what government did what, that the former Government did nothing, and so on. Before he was here a few things were done by the former Government for the Atlantic area in particular, and certainly for the whole of Canada. Among them was the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, which has been a godsend to an area such as mine, especially where we have a thermal power plant where subsidies are paid to these consumers of electricity in the Atlantic area who take electricity which comes from a thermal power plant which uses coal. This has helped us a great deal. There were other ways in which the Atlantic Provinces were helped. There was the decentralization of industry, and providing naval work for the Atlantic area. This sort of help was given to a great extent.
The Minister perhaps has some knowledge of these things. He was not concerned with the particular industry I had in mind at the
June 29, 1965

time, but in the days of the former Government there was projected the move-and the former Government went along with and encouraged this proposal-whereby at the time Canada Car was closed in Montreal, the machinery and facilities were moved from there to the Trenton plants. This was a godsend to the constituency I represent. The former Government was under much pressure not to move this plant and to let it carry on where it was. But the move was made and it has helped a great deal in that area, it being the biggest industry there.
I hope that the bill the Minister will bring forward will spell out in detail what these grants will mean so far as co-operation with Industrial Estates and other provincial bodies throughout Canada are concerned. At that time we will be able better to tell just what this measure will mean. But, Mr. Chairman, I do hope that these grants will go further than the original legislation, which was to give a tax free holiday for three years and the accelerated depreciation, and will assist getting industry into designated areas.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few words I would like to say before the resolution carries. I must say that I am as curious as other hon. Members to see the bill, in order to ascertain whether the Government has learned anything from its experience in the past. We in the Province of Saskatchewan have failed to benefit from any of the legislation the Government has brought forward along this line in the past. In view of recent representations made by our Premier and his Minister of Natural Resources, I am very hopeful that when the bill is introduced it will reflect that measure of co-operation and understanding on the part of the Government and the Minister concerned that will give a truly national outlook to this legislation and its application to industry.
I would be remiss in my duty if I did not go back to the period of the Second World War and point out what took place at that time with regard to the centralization of industry. I do not want to criticize the Government of that day for what it did then; but if this legislation is to reinforce the mistakes that were made at that time and perpetuate a situation in which industry was centralized in certain areas of this country,
Interim Supply
to the detriment of other areas where perhaps some natural resources were more readily available than in the area that was affected, then I would think the legislation would be lacking in the respect that we in western Canada would like to see corrected.
I cannot help but think of my own Province of Saskatchewan and the loss of population there; perhaps I should not say the loss of population altogether, but the limitation of growth that has resulted from what happened during the last Great War and the period immediately following. We have failed to achieve an increase in population of approximately half a million people, in a period when other parts of the country have been growing, largely because of the centralization of industry that was encouraged during that particular period. I hope that the bill will be broad enough to take into consideration the truly national needs of our country in this regard, and will restore to the prairie region in western Canada some of the incentives that have been lacking during the past many years. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, without saying anything further in this regard at this particular time I will await the introduction of the bill. [DOT] (9:30 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two points which I think should be covered before the House proceeds to take an adjournment, and I can think of no better time than at 25 minutes to ten on a warm summer evening, after other dramatic events have taken place, to share with the Committee my views on such matters. One portfolio which any New Brunswick Member would be proud to discuss at this time of night is that of public works.
There are two points I wish to make here. One is that the Government has failed to complete roads to resources projects which have been started during the last few years. This is a co-operative scheme between the Government of Canada and the governments of the provinces. Yet the location of the various roads and whether or not they are to be completed is decided at the whim of the provincial administrations. I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Public Works two projects which, by a strange coincidence, happen to be located in my constituency. One of them is popularly known as the Kingston peninsula trail. This road has been under way for the past six years. In answer to an inquiry of mine directed to the Ministry I find that no steps are being taken this year to finish the remaining 12 miles of this tourist attraction.
Then there is a very important road to resource between the communities of Chip-man in the County of Queens, in the constituency of Royal, and the community of

Doaktown. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works would have just as much interest as I in the completion of this road, which is very much needed by the lumbering community.
The second point with regard to public works which I should like to make concerns the absence of any announced Government policy of assistance to marinas and other boating facilities along navigable waters. The Minister of Northern Affairs on the radio last night spoke of water as being the most important of our resources. I am one who believes that this is the fact, and in this regard I am saddened to think of the great Saint John water system. Some years ago, in the thirties, we had a program of construction of public wharves. In those days it used to be thought that these wharves should have a commercial use, in the narrow sense of the word. I regret to say that I have been unable to persuade the Government, in these days when so many people have the use of motorboats and other pleasure craft, that this type of use should also be regarded as commercial use.
The Saint John River system has some 60 public wharves owned by the Queen in the right of Canada, and I think that it is tragic that a vigorous policy of exploitation has not been embarked upon by the Government to enable people with leisure, among whom I should like to think Members of Parliament may soon fall if events take their proper course, to enjoy the unmatched beauties, if I may be chauvinistic, of the Saint John River system.
These two matters are very close to the constituency of Royal, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to move to another area to which I think the Government should pay more than lip service, namely the subject of university education. This subject has been the pet of a great many Members and I should like to say that the interest is not restricted to Members of this party. As a matter of fact, I think it has been almost a backbench crusade, with one exception, and that exception was the late hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, who made many important speeches on the subject of the negligence, which is what it was really, of the Government in failing to provide any increase in assistance to Canadian universities.
The Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary have replied to questions of mine and of other hon. Members by saying that the Government is awaiting the results of the Bladen Commission before announcing policy.
June 29, 1965

This of course is the typical answer of a Government which does not wish to take any responsibility; it finds some commission and hides behind it, not announcing any policy. This Government, which came into office on votes gained by promises of bold and daring acts for all our people, has really shown a curious lack of policy in connection with higher education in this country. Those of us who like not only to fight politics at the constituency level but also like to stand back once in a while and philosophize about politics, find it curious that here we have a party which prides itself on its appeal to the intellectual levels of the country and which tosses about fancy phrases, yet when the issue is joined no government in recent Canadian history has done less-in fact this Government has done nothing-for higher education in Canada than this one. At least there has been no increase in assistance. Yet the Government has received briefs from the Canadian Universities Foundation, one as early as May, 1963 and another as of December, 1963. During the intervening period of time other submissions have been made.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
It is also a curiosity in this country that there is no one on the staff anywhere in the ministry of Canada, at the federal level- I want to be fair, but I think this is a fair statement-who really has the responsibility for enunciating or recommending policy to the Government of Canada about higher education. For a short while the Government had the benefit of the services of Mr. Kenneth Taylor but, if my memory serves me correctly, this individual has not been part of the public service for at least a year.
So here we have a Government that spends I think not quite four tenths of 1 per cent of the national budget on higher education, and coupled with this shocking figure is the absence of any spokesman for higher education in the public service.
The university students of my province staged a wonderful democratic protest, in the best traditions of a public protest, in front of the legislature in our province following the announcement that the fees of the provincial University of New Brunswick were to be raised because of the lack of action on the part of the federal Government. I am also aware of the complaints of the undergraduates at Mount Allison University, and at many of the universities of Nova Scotia.
There are several persons adorning the Government benches, some of whom are in the Ministry, who have had a role to play as
Interim, Supply
teachers and professors in our Maritime universities. Yet, to use a well worn cliche, they sit idly by with a smile on their faces while this problem is allowed to deteriorate. Mari-timers should be glad to know that the Prime Minister of Canada intends to travel to one of our Maritime universities, in mid-July I think, to receive an honorary degree. I hope in his statement, comments or speech, if he is to make one-or at least in his dialogue which is another well-worn current cliche- he will bring about a change of heart in university circles, which has existed for the last few years, which will make them believe that this Government is the able and daring Government which publicity emanators promised it would be.
The serious thing is that undergraduates are getting ready now-this is the time of year- to enter our universities; yet this Government has done nothing upon which university administrators or the young people of this country can pattern themselves or plan for the forthcoming academic year. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance whether he has received any protests from student university groups about the increases of fees that have been announced, not only in my own part of Canada but also in western Canada, where there has been general objection taken. Has the Minister received any representations from university presidents or representatives of university administrators, respecting the policy of the Government, to upgrade the per capita grant to the very minimum of the often suggested three dollar figure in time for the next academic year? This would be a dramatic gesture that could take place and which would receive the general approval, I am sure, of all Members, before we go home to our constituencies.
Mr. Chairman, if the Minister is about to make such an announcement, I will be glad to yield the floor so that he can capture some of the drama of this day, by doing something that he should do for Canada.
He is not even listening.

Of course he is not listening, but I know that tomorrow he will have a precis of this compelling speech placed on his desk, so that he will be able to formulate a reply to appease the people of this country, so in turn they will know that the Government has not been negligent in respect of higher education.
Now that the universities have had a comment or two from me, I have one last comment to make on interim supply which has

June 29, 1965
Interim Supply
to do with the truly extraordinary things that are going on in the City of Montreal in relation to Expo '67. I am astounded by the concept of Expo '67, and I think that many of the events that are planned for that great exposition will be really wonderful evidence of the progress that Canada has made. I must confess, however, that I am one of those who derive neither aesthetic nor any other thrill from the strange projection the Mayor of Montreal is going to erect into the skyline of that city, provided President de Gaulle still wants to co-operate in this strange misuse of public funds. I hope the funds of the Government of Canada are not going to be spent in this attempt to reach for the stars, that is being planned for that city. Surely there are many other things that we can plan which may be useful, on a permanent basis, to the general population of Canada.
Someone suggested that perhaps the facilities could be used for a university campus. I am not able to make any judgment as to whether or not that is a sensible suggestion, but I think 1 am as competent as anybody else to judge whether or not this strange thing that is going to be projected into the sky is a waste of money. I suppose I will receive a slick comment from the Expo officials telling me exactly what this projection-I cannot use the word I intended to use-has to do with Man and his World in 1967.
I was somewhat upset by the appeal made by Mr. Kniewasser-I hope I have pronounced his name correctly, but it does not matter because it will be transcribed in Hansard correctly-for $30 million from private industry, as was announced in the Montreal Gazette of June 23. Apparently he wants this amount of money from private industry so that Expo '67 can carry on its plan. Mr. Kniewasser in his appeal said that this amount was necessary because of the reluctance of some major industries to come forward with donations. I am sure the reluctance on the part of industry is the result of the unusual nature of this clause.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I do not, of course, expect that it will be possible to do so before we adjourn for the summer but certainly when we return after the summer recess a great many people will want to have the opportunity to look at a very detailed report of costs, to date. I had hoped that this would be possible earlier so that the upset industry is experiencing about Expo '67 could be somewhat allayed by this

information. If Expo '67 is not to become a white elephant it should have the very diligent and vigilant scrutiny of Treasury Board, for instance, and all the other manifestations of good government accounting practices.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
I would be delighted to have a question.

I know the hon. Member would not want to misrepresent the situation or do any harm to the cause of Expo. Is he aware that what Mr. Kniewasser was talking about was not the rising costs of Expo in the sense in which the hon. Member was speaking, but the rising costs of construction?
One of my colleagues suggests that if we did not have the 11 per cent tax on construction material and equipment-
Imposed by the Government.

I am getting lots of advice at this late hour of the night from my colleagues-construction costs might not be as great. I do not think it really matters, to my argument, whether it is construction costs that are rising or what is rising. All I know is that the Montreal Gazette of June 23 last had this headline: "Expo Searches For $30 Million To Keep Three Projected Pavilions". Over one story there is a subheading, "M.P. Renews Demand For Probe" and over another story by Bill Bantey there is the subheading "Kniewasser Appeals to Canadian Business". The story follows and hon. Members can read it to their own satisfaction.
But I think there is some public concern about Expo, and just because we stand here and ask questions we should not be considered to be against the project. I for one think it is a most imaginative project but, like any other project, I think we should be able to know roughly, within say $20 million or $30 million, what the eventual cost of Expo '67 will be. I do not think this is an unrealistic or unparliamentary request for one to make.
I have covered various facets of interim supply and I hope that tomorrow afternoon there will be some answers from the ministry with regard to some of the problems I have posed. Most important to Canada as a whole, of course, is the problem facing our universities. Because I have a great interest in my own constituency I should also like to think
June 29, 1965

that the Minister of Public Works will answer my questions about the roads to resources program and also an imaginative program for the use of the Saint John River. Because I should like to think that Expo '67 has the wholehearted approval, understanding and sympathy of the business community as well as all Members of Parliament, I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce will want to calm the fears of a good many people about this project. We will leave it to the President of France to decide whether a tower will be constructed to spoil what is otherwise the rather lovely skyline of the great City of Montreal.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to add a postscript to the remarks I made yesterday on interim supply when I raised the question of William Grant, former Yukon agent of the Indian Affairs Department. I received the news today that his colleague, Joseph Armishaw, who was also charged, has been found not guilty on all charges. This man was suspended as of September, 1963. The charges were only laid on November 4, 1964. He too has been without salary and has had to fall back on whatever resources he could scrape up. One can readily understand how difficult it would be for a civil servant to obtain interim employment when he is under suspension.
Some people seem to think that undue influence was used in regard to these cases. I want to say again that I am amazed at the humanity expressed in certain cases but which did not apply in regard to these two cases. Therefore I trust that before we conclude interim supply we will get an answer with regard to Grant and Armishaw.
I received today a news item from Edmonton stating that Jean Dastous, director of administration in the Department of Indian Affairs, has said in reply to an inquiry that William Grant cannot be returned to his previous job because there was a separation. Does this mean that the man has been fired? To me the word "separation" means only
Interim Supply
one thing, that he has been dismissed from the service or has been pressured into resigning.
We want to know precisely what is happening in this regard, in the light of the comments by the judge and in the light of the comments by the people of the community. We are not content with just being given the decision of some man here in Ottawa far removed from the scene. We know there have been very strong comments by the Justices of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory with regard to the bureaucratic machine that has to do with northern administration, and certainly I should not like to be in the shoes of those people who are the butt, shall we say, of the criticism of these two Justices, both of whom know the north country and both of whom are eminent lawyers. One was appointed by a former Liberal administration. I refer to Mr. Justice Sissons who used to be a Member of this House. Mr. Justice Parker had a long career in the Northwest Territories before appointment. Surely these men know what they are talking about. Yet it seems that the words of these men and the words of other people in that area fall on deaf ears when they strike Ottawa.
It had also been my understanding that the Minister of Justice was going to reply to remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition concerning a Justice of the Province of Ontario and one in the Province of Quebec whose positions are under review. A statement was promised. Are we going to have it before supply is granted?
Ten o'clock.

I trust that the Minister of National Revenue is making note of all these things and that replies will be given tomorrow.
I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.
